RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT INDIAN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What action, in detail, has been taken with respect to each of the following recommendations of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Indian affairs:
"(a) Indian affairs should be the subject of a dominion-provincial conference in order that such matters may be transferred to provincial jurisdiction as may be mutually acceptable to the Indian people, provincial and federal authorities.
(b)	Another special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons should be appointed within a period of seven years to review Indian affairs.
(c)	A program of research into the economic, cultural and social concepts of the Indian people should be undertaken in conjunction with the provinces and universities.
(d)	Community planning and development studies should be continued.'1?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT INDIAN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
(a) The administration of Indian affairs was on the agenda of the federal-provincial conference held in Ottawa in November, 1963. It was agreed that a federal-provincial ministerial conference on Indian affairs be convened in 1964. Although the month of May was suggested as the most suitable time, it was not possible to complete the planning in time. However, planning is continuing and the conference will be held later in the year.
(b)	No action is being taken to recommend another special committee of the Senate and House of Commons to review Indian affairs at this time as the seven year period referred to in this recommendation will not be reached until 1968. The establishing of such a joint committee will be a matter for parliament to decide.
(c)	A national Indian research project to assess the participation by Indians in the social and economic life of the country is being undertaken by Dr. H. B. Hawthorn of

Questions
the University of British Columbia as director and Dr. Adelard Tremblay of Laval University as associate director. The research will cover four major areas concerning Indians: economic development; advancement in education; responsibilities that exist at various government levels; and band councils and the development of self government. It is expected that the research project will be completed in 1966.
(d)	Increasing attention has been given to community planning and development studies in recent years. An economic development study for the Blood Indian reserve has been carried out. This includes demographic analyses, studies on mineral resources, soils, range, agriculture, forestry, etc. Studies for the economic development of Indians in the Patricia district of Ontario have been carried out in collaboration with the provincial department of lands and forests. A preliminary inventory of Indian reserve resources is now in progress.

subtopic: AIR POLLUTION RESEARCH
AIR POLLUTION RESEARCH
speechtext:
Huron):
1.	Is the Department of National Health and Welfare conducting a program of research on air pollution and, if so, what have been the findings of this program as to its cause in connection with (a) the motor car, the truck and the bus (b) industrial and commercial enterprise (c) nuclear fall-out?
2.	Have any conclusions been arrived at as to methods of control?
3.	How much has this program cost to date?
[Mr. Laprise.l

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AIR POLLUTION RESEARCH
speechtext:
1. Yes.
(a)	Motor car. The principal cause of air pollution from the motor car is the emission of unburned fuel or hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, oxides of nitrogen, sulphur dioxide, organic compounds such as aldehydes, acids, alcohols, esters, phenols, carcinogens and others, smoke and particulate matter, including lead.
Truck and bus. Similar to above for those operating on gasoline. Diesel engines produce much lower or negligible concentrations of carbon monoxide for all operating conditions; except acceleration or other heavy load conditions. However diesel emissions of hydrocarbons and oxides of nitrogen, expressed in lbs. per hour, are greater in all cases than the values for gasoline engines. Odour and irritation of diesel exhaust are due principally to the content of aldehydes.
(b)	Industrial and commercial enterprises. Causes of air pollution from this source are many and varied, depending upon the nature of the enterprise. Combustion products of solid fuels may pollute the air with smoke, fly ash up to 10 per cent of the fuel used, sulphur oxides, oxides of nitrogen, hydrocarbons, organic acids and aldehydes and many other products. Liquid fuels in combustion contribute very much less ash, but similar quantities of sulphur oxides, depending upon the sulphur content of the fuel, and products similar to those mentioned above. Gaseous fuels contain no ash or sulphur and produce the least quantity of contaminants during combustion.
Some of the major contaminants from industrial enterprises are sulphur dioxide from smelting of sulphide concentrates; odorous sulphur compounds from pulp and paper mills; fluorides from aluminium defining and phosphate fertilizer production; sulphur dioxide, other odorous sulphur compounds, hydrocarbons and catalyst dust from oil refining; arsenic from roasting of arsenical gold ores; oxides of nitrogen and ammonia from manufacture of nitric acid and nitration products; chlorine from electrolysis of salt; lead from battery plants and smelters; zinc from metallurgical plants; iron oxide dust and sulphur dioxide from iron and steel manufacturing; dust from cement manufacture and other crushing, grinding and sintering or roasting operations. Almost every industrial process gives rise to air contamination of one form or another.
(c)	Nuclear fall-out. As part of its comprehensive radioactive fall-out study program, the Department of National Health and Welfare has, with the co-operation of the meteorological services branch of the Department of Transport, established a program

of air and precipitation sampling and analysis for radioactive fall-out. A network of 24 sampling stations provides the Department of National Health and Welfare with: (a) 24 hour air filter samples, daily; (b) accumulated rainfall and snowfall samples, monthly. These samples are analysed for total fall-out activity and the precipitation samples are further analyzed for strontium 89, strontium 90 and caesium 137. Results are published monthly in Data from Radiation Protection Programs (a copy of the latest issue of which was tabled in the house on May 20). Fall-out levels at any station or any part of the country are governed by nuclear weapons testing programs and by meteorological conditions, they are not known to contribute to air pollution in the sense that motor cars and industrial and commercial enterprises do.
2.	(a) Methods of control for motor vehicles. Intensive studies on various control systems have been under way in the United States by the public health service, the state of California, the automobile manufacturers association in Detroit and other organizations for some years. These systems include the design of new engine processes, improved carburetor design and catalytic or flame combustion of exhaust gas by means of an afterburner. The state of California has established performance requirements for the control of contaminants in exhaust of motor vehicles but no system has been approved for installation as yet. The Department of National Health and Welfare is keeping abreast of such developments.
A partial palliative has been found in the installation of a crankcase control device to prevent air pollution from engine blowby gas. This device is now manufactured for installation in the United States.
(b) Control methods for industrial and commercial enterprises. Remedial measures and control systems have been designed for the collection of dusts or mists and the absorption of many gaseous contaminants. Solid or liquid particulates may be removed from stack gases by electrostatic precipitation, venturi or other scrubbers, cyclone collectors, fibrous filters or sonic agglomeration. Sulphur dioxide from smelting and sintering operations may be converted to sulphuric acid and phosphate fertilizers. Fluorides may be removed by wet scrubbers. Odorous compounds and solvent vapours may be burned by catalytic combustion or removed by activated carbon. In some cases the recovered products can be returned to the process or converted economically to valuable by-products. However research is being conducted in many countries on the development of processes for the removal of sulphur dioxide,
20220-255J
Questions
oxides of nitrogen and other contaminants occurring in low concentrations in flue gases, especially those from thermal power plants. The Department of National Health and Welfare is being kept informed regarding such developments.
(c) Control of nuclear fall-out in air can be effected by termination of atmospheric nuclear weapons testing.
3. The air pollution program was initiated in 1956 within the occupational health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare and has cost about $400,000 since that time. The program is closely integrated with air pollution control activities of provincial health departments.
The radioactive fall-out study program was initiated in 1959 within the radiation protection division of the Department of National Health and Welfare and has cost approximately $100,000 since that time.

show that imports from the United States increased by 17.5 per cent from the first quarter of 1963 to the first quarter of 1964 whereas imports from all sources increased by 17.6 per cent. Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Calgary North asked how many Canadian army and air force personnel were still in the Congo and when were they to be returned to Canada.
As the hon. member knows, under the resolution adopted by the general assembly on October 18, 1963, the United Nations force in the Congo will be terminated at the end of this month. Repatriation of Canadian personnel has already started, with some 54 returning to Canada on May 27. At the present time there is a total of 179 Canadian servicemen in the Congo. speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS
speechtext:
Here are the facts concerning the case of John Thomadakis.
Thomadakis is a citizen of Greece who was engaged as a shipmate in the United States, on January 1962, and who jumped his ship in Montreal on June 6, 1962.
He succeeded in escaping the searching efforts of immigration officers until March 3, 1964, when he was arrested in Toronto.
An investigation was held the next day under the Immigration Act. Contrary to some reports, Thomadakis was made aware of the purpose of the investigation and he admitted that he understood why the investigation was held. A Greek female interpreter was present and Thomadakis said he was certain she had the necessary qualifications to interpret his statements. He was informed of his right to be represented by a lawyer of his choice, and he stated under oath that he did not want to be represented.
The facts brought out at the investigation established that Thomadakis had entered Canada by avoiding the examination and that having come to Canada as crew member, he stayed here after the ship on which he had come went away. The special investigator then ordered his deportation, as required by the act.
Although Thomadakis stated that he did not wish to exercise his right of appeal, a stenographic copy of the evidence was sent to the headquarters of the immigration branch. The case was studied again in Ottawa and the deportation order was confirmed. Thomadakis was informed by letter, under date of March 18, that he would be deported to Greece as soon as it would be feasible.
Since Thomadakis had nothing to prove that he was a Greek citizen, steps were taken to get the document needed for the trip and arrangements were made for the trip.
Before those arrangements could be completed, however, Thomadakis had an interview with the R.C.M.P. They informed him that he would be charged with illegal entry into Canada and he received formal notification from them. Once again a competent interpreter was present and Thomadakis admitted that the statement read to him in Greek was accurate.
Thomadakis was served a summons on April 9, 1964, and on April 10 he was charged by the police with illegal entry into Canada. He was found guilty in magistrate's court in Toronto and sentenced to five months in jail.
Hon. members will notice that in that case appropriate legal action was taken by the immigration authorities within 24 hours
Inquiries of the Ministry of Thomadakis' arrest, that a competent interpreter was provided, that his right to be represented by counsel was clearly explained to him and that he was given the opportunity to appeal the decision of the special investigator. In my opinion, no justifiable criticism can be made concerning the handling of the case, and there have been no undue delays with respect to arrangements for deportation.
However, by entering Canada illegally, Thomadakis was not only liable to deportation; he had committed a felony. He was liable to prosecution in that respect as for any offence against the law of Canada. At present he is serving the sentence imposed by the court and will be deported upon his release from jail.
I could add that a certain number of prisoners in the Don jail have been convicted by a competent court for crimes they have committed and that they will be deported from Canada when they have served their sentence.

speechtext:
National Housing Act
If the minister will ask his officials I am sure in 10 or 15 minutes there can be explained to him the history of the long fight which we waged from roughly 1950 through to 1958 for an amelioration of the restrictive terms of the housing act so that it would work in the Yukon Territory. He will then immediately understand just how difficult it was in that day for northerners to obtain loans at all. But with all credit to the previous government, the act was amended so as to permit building, and I think the significance of the statistic I have just cited to the minister will indicate that this is so; that is to say, where only two homes were built under the N.H.A. prior to 1958, in the next two or three year period there were well over 100 built in the Whitehorse area alone. But there is still no N.H.A. building going on in any other community in the Yukon.
The reason for this, of course, is that the standards are too high. Some communities have not water and sewer facilities; septic tanks are not allowed, I believe. I am not an expert on the housing standards that are required by C.M.H.C., but I do know that one of the greatest complaints as I travel around my constituency is that the people who want to build homes and settle down and make themselves and their families permanent citizens there simply cannot do so because they have not the wherewithal themselves with which to build, and N.H.A. is not working in their communities.
Therefore I would urge the minister to give these northern conditions particular consideration. The personnel of C.M.H.C. are not only dedicated people, but in my experience they are people of imagination who can usually find solutions to these problems if they really have a mind to do so. I am sure if a little bit of time is devoted to this particular problem they will be able to come up with suggestions to the minister for perhaps future amendments to the act which would allow home building to go on in these northern communities to the same extent as it goes on in the remaining parts of Canada.
The other matter I wanted to draw to the minister's attention is the lack of any inspection facilities in the Yukon; and the same situation, again, exists in the Northwest Territories. Usually, as the minister knows, inspection services are available in or close to communities that are doing any extensive C.M.H.C. building at all. The facilities that we are required to use in the Yukon are based at Prince George, so that there is a substantial delay between reaching the stage of construction that the act requires and its actual inspection, for which the inspector must travel from Prince George to Whitehorse, and then the approval and subsequent

payment. So contractors sometimes have to-wait as long as two or three months, and longer, for progress payments. Certainly it is wrong, I feel, to have contractors carrying the corporation or the government-the corporation in this instance-out of their own funds. That is what it amounts to. The mortgage advances are not made, and the contractor has to obtain a loan at the bank at 6 per cent in order to make the payment which C.M.H.C. should have made. If the inspection services were based on the spot this problem would be overcome.
I submitted a rather lengthy list of suggestions concerning standards to Mr. Bates before his death. Mr. Bates replied at length to me, and I understand that these matters are all under consideration in the corporation now so I will not take up the time of the house with the detail of those submissions. I have never had anything but the greatest co-operation from the officials of C.M.H.C., and particularly Mr. Bates with whom I was wont to deal most often. I am sure they will look at these submissions with respect to standards and perhaps, if it is at all possible, make the necessary proposals to have the standards requirements of their legislation or regulations amended so as to take into account northern conditions.
With those few observations with respect to northern housing, Mr. Speaker, I would urge the minister to take these specific matters under his personal care and attention. I know he will do that, and I know he will get the utmost co-operation from the officials of C.M.H.C., and perhaps we might see some further progress in northern housing development.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has already been indicated by other speakers from my party, we welcome this bill and are, of course, prepared to support it. It is particularly pleasant to be able to accept this measure with enthusiasm, because I recall that the last time the hon. gentleman brought some legislation before the house in connection with the post office we were not able to greet it with the same enthusiasm with which we welcome this bill, and that is a pleasant change.
I do not want to deal with the specific clauses of the bill. We had some discussion on this matter, and I want to leave the clauses until the committee stage where they will be dealt with in detail by the minister. One thing which is important in the discussion is this. It should be made clear that the problems of housing and urban development are in no way exclusively restricted to the large centres of population; the smaller

towns in the rural areas are just as vitally affected by measures of this kind as the large city centres.
A report by the Ontario department of municipal affairs in 1962 set out this situation very clearly. For example, it pointed out that in Sault Ste. Marie 55 per cent of the structures were classified as less than good. The survey conducted in the city of Kingston again showed evidence of blight. The survey showed that many of the homes were seriously lacking in necessary facilities for good housing. Hamilton had pockets of substandard housing, which was also set out in the report. In Windsor over 25,000 structures were examined, 13.3 per cent found vulnerable to blight, 3 per cent totally blighted and others partly blighted. The report also discusses Ottawa, where out of 5,385 units examined there were 4,370 which had serious deficiencies in sanitary and housing facilities.
One of the worst places in the province of Ontario, and perhaps in all Canada, is my home city of Toronto, where very little progress has been made in the matter of public housing in the last five years. In 1958 the metropolitan council set itself a target of 1,000 units a year but now, five years later, they have only erected about 550 in total.
This is a situation which has developed all across the country; it is not restricted. It is in contrast to some other areas which have promoted this type of housing very adequately and have therefore been much more successful. The city of Newark in New Jersey has built twice as many as the whole of Canada, yet its population is only 500,000 compared with Canada's 18 million.
We were particularly pleased to hear in the minister's speech the emphasis he properly laid on the need for public housing and urban redevelopment, because these are two of the areas which have been tremendously neglected. The minister was very tactful in his speech, and admitted quite candidly that progress to date had been something less than perfect. That is a diplomatic way of putting it. I suggest instead that to date it has really been an abject failure. One of the problems we seem to have in this house and which I have experienced is that everyone seems reluctant to admit that problems exist in case they start an argument as to who created the problem, and we seem to spend as much time trying to allocate responsibility for a particular problem and in blaming the cause on a particular government as we do in trying to devise some sort of effective and realistic programs to deal with them.
My main interest in participating in this debate at the second reading stage is that I
National Housing Act
feel what we should be concerning ourselves with is not just the passage of this bill but with what is going to happen after the bill receives royal assent. Words and phrases do not build houses, and the good intentions expressed in the bill are absolutely useless unless they are carried out with tremendous initiative, energy and vigour. I think we should be more concerned about how this bill is carried into reality than with the clauses themselves, and I will suggest to the minister some proposals for his consideration which I think will enable us to make this an act really worth while and productive of concrete results.
The first thing I think the government should seriously consider is the creation of a ministry of housing which should be headed by a full time minister. For too long in Canada we have failed to recognize that good housing, at prices which people can afford, and good citizens are intimately connected; that the provision of good housing is every bit as important as the provision of family allowances, pensions, hospitalization schemes and other welfare measures. We have paid lip service to this principle in Canada, but I do not think we have ever really accepted it. Yet the connection between housing and good citizens is so obvious to me that I do not think it needs any documentation.
Governments in previous years have largely regarded housing as some sort of economic pump primer. When construction was dragging our governments have tended to turn on the tap and let some mortgage money flow out in an endeavour to stimulate the housing industry, not so much through a genuine belief in a housing scheme as an inducement to employment and as a means of attempting to stimulate the economy. We saw an example of that in the $500 winter construction bonus, which was primarily designed to provide employment and was not particularly concerned with housing itself. It is also significant that this scheme is not administered by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under the minister but is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour.
Over the years our housing agencies have been shifted from one department to another, and they are now under the control of the present minister. Presumably when another minister is appointed after the by-election in Saskatoon there will be another shifting around. This has really lowered the whole approach to housing.
I do not think we have ever recognized the tremendous need in Canada for a genuine national housing program. I know it is difficult. I realize that housing problems have to be worked out in the context of the federal

National Housing Act
state, and that we have to deal with provinces which have been pretty darned apathetic over the problem. We have also had to deal with municipalities which are the creatures of those provinces. I realize that our municipal politicians in particular and people in general have always shown a great reluctance to get into the field of housing, and I am aware of the difficulties this creates for a federal minister who is trying to promote a proper housing scheme. But the best way to show the provinces and the municipalities that one really means business would be to give pretty serious consideration to elevating housing to its proper place. This is just as important as national health and welfare, it is just as important as fisheries and it is just as important as forestry.
I think it is about time that we Canadians establish and put into operation a new ministry of housing headed by a full-time minister. In view of the hon. gentlemen's speech at the resolution stage and the attitude he has shown, I think I would be quite happy if he were the minister in charge of this great undertaking. So my first suggestion is that we have a full-time minister of housing.
My second suggestion is that I think the minister should be prepared to take to the road and sell this measure to the provinces and to the municipalities. This is going to be one of the very big problems, to overcome what I described a moment ago as the apathy and indifference of the provinces and the municipalities in this field. I should like to see, for example, a series of provincial-municipal conferences organized by the minister in each province where the provincial governments and the municipalities could be brought together, and their needs examined and in particular specific goals and targets set so that we will have some rule by which to measure the success which is being achieved in this particular field. Again, if this is going to be done, if you are really going to get out, promote the act and overcome the apathy, there will have to be a full-time minister of housing. I do not see how you are going to get around that particular problem otherwise.
Third, I should like to see the minister stir up his own department, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which at the moment is largely oriented toward private, single family homes and apartments built by private operators. This is not the department's fault. Successive governments have never really encouraged the department to activate itself in some of these other fields. But they are at the moment largely oriented in this direction, and it seems to me that one thing that really could promote the act would be if the minister could get the department all steamed up, and then

C.M.H.C. officials right across the country could really sell the program to the municipal officials and local planners with whom they are in daily contact. This would go a long way toward active promotion of this particular scheme.
Fourth, I think the government should seriously consider sponsoring and financing courses on a university level for housing authorities, housing administrators, welfare authorities and, in short, anybody having anything to do with public housing, especially homes for the aged. If such courses were made available and the details, benefits and necessity of substantial action under this act were made clear, I think these officials would have a lot of information they do not have now. They would be a lot better informed and prepared to recommend schemes to their particular municipalities.
Fifth, I should like to see the minister promote this housing legislation by greater use of press conferences and press coverage. We simply must begin to make Canadians more housing conscious. We are obsessed in Canada with single family ownership and all of the advertising and promotion have been in this direction. Consequently a stigma has grown up against subsidized public housing, and I think the minister has a big job ahead of him if he is going to reorient Canadian thinking on this subject and make people realize that public housing is perfectly respectable, and subsidized housing is economically necessary. If he began such a campaign I think it would be most helpful.
For example, I should like to see a model city built somewhere in Canada so all Canadians could see the wonderful new things that are available in town planning, planning techniques and housing in general. We might even make it a part of our centennial celebrations; but a model city would encourage people to see it, make them realize the importance of housing in our daily lives and would put them a long way on the road to considering this as a major problem.
Sixth, I should like to see the government initiate a crash program for senior citizens, especially single pensioners. I know the minister has been on a cross country tour and has visited many areas. I am sure he has seen, as all of us have, the shameful and disgusting accommodation in which many pensioners live. All of us during election campaigns have had occasion to visit these individuals in their single rooms at the top of houses and have come away-I did at least-ashamed to be a Canadian, in that we were permitting our pensioners to live in such deplorable circumstances. While I realize there are other aspects of great importance, I should still like to see a crash program, for humanitarian

reasons if nothing else, because these people are not going to be with us very much longer.
Seventh, we simply must find some method of streamlining and making less complicated the procedures and regulations required to initiate these proposals. At the present time it takes approximately 58 steps in number to bring a program into actual realization. This results in endless and needless delays, frustration and quite often eventual abandonment of the project because it just does not seem to be going to get anywhere.
Eighth, we have to try to convince municipalities that they must permit greater flexibility in building, greater flexibility in their bylaws, greater flexibility in the designing of the buildings involved. I think Toronto has the most archaic building bylaws in North America, and I am sure this sort of thing frustrates and defeats many of the purposes of the planners and many of the hopes of our legislators.
Ninth, finally, and most important, I think that everything devolves on the minister. It seems to me that the success or failure of the act will rest on his ability to marshal his energy and imagination and to give the country leadership in the field of housing, something that it has been badly lacking. The problems of urban communities are so immense that they are almost staggering. I do not suggest for a moment that we can expect any miracles in the next year or two, but it is time for action to commence, and it really is going to devolve on the minister himself. In fact, the minister has an opportunity that I would envy, because if he is able to do some of these things, if he is able to overcome the apathy, if he is able to get things moving in the housing field in a really big way, he has a chance to change the face of Canada and to begin now that process that has been long delayed and which would revive our urban centres and our rural regions as well.
These suggestions I make to the minister are obviously of a short run character designed to deal with this particular piece of legislation, but in concluding I want to suggest something else. I suggest to him that the real problem of urban life is, as I have said, enormously complicated because it involves all the needs of town planning, transportation, communication, industrialization, commercialization, as well as places for people to live. It creates great social and psychological problems which none of us really understands and we do not have enough information with which to deal with them. I propose that the minister should give consideration to a long run approach to housing in addition to this legislation. I suggest to him that the government should consider appointing a royal commission on housing that could begin to
National Housing Act
sit now and obtain the information we need to devise solutions to deal with the problems of urban Canada in the next two decades.
We all know that our urban areas are growing steadily in numbers and strength, and that it will not be too long before 80 per cent of our people will live in cities and 20 per cent in rural districts. This is going to pose problems of an almost staggering nature. I suggest that this royal commission should have wide ranging terms of reference. For example, I think it should establish the approximate housing needs of low income families. I should recommend a national housing policy to deal with all segments of society including the following: Housing for low income families, housing for moderate income families and housing for the elderly.
It should study and report on the kind of public housing programs required in large, medium and small communities. It should study and report on the place of government in land assembly and economic rental housing projects, because we have really never made up our minds what position the government occupies. It should study and report on a less complicated arrangement with respect to financial and accounting arrangements as between the participating groups. It should study and report on rental structures on all types of public housing. It should report on the present system of producing public housing; how effective it is, what the roadblocks are and what is the best way around them. It should report on the desirability of the senior governments acting as financial agents only, giving greater and greater autonomy to our municipal people, to the local agencies and corporations that will carry out these projects. It should report on the role to be played by private enterpise in urban renewal and public housing programs. We have really not delineated where the government stands and where private enterpise stands, and this is constantly muddling up and confusing housing projects.
This commission should study and report on the general planning of public housing projects with specific reference to design, size, provision of services, relation to urban development programs, conservation, rehabilitation and acquisition of existing housing, all the things that go into a massive plan. It should give some idea of the kind of local organization required to deal with urban renewal, public housing and relocation operations. I believe that as this act comes into force in the next two or three years, as it gets more active, we will have an organization. However, what we really need is a thorough study in depth. It should report on housing for the aged with specific reference to environment and site requirements and

National Housing Act
co-operation between the various levels of government, as well as economics, the plight of our pensioners and their needs.
These are only a few of the things I think this commission should study. If this commission were appointed and permitted to sit for the next two or three years gathering this information in the usual way, then I believe the government would have the necessary information with which to initiate, not a short term program which is of course essential at the moment, but a long term program that is really designed to assess the whole problem of the development of urban Canada and the best way in which we, as the government, can handle it. I know that is a big task and that is why I reluctantly suggest a royal commission. I do not usually like them. However, I think this is the type of work they can usefully do. If the minister would take this into consideration I think we could possibly come up with a long range program.
I just want to repeat what I said at the beginning. We are glad to have the act and we are relying on the minister to give the government the leadership it so desperately needs. I believe that if this is done, then despite the problems we may be on the way to a solution of them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker we, too, welcome the improvements that are going to be introduced as a result of this bill we have before us. Like everyone else, I suppose, we can always find more things to do than we have the means with which to accomplish them. I am well aware, as I think most members are, of the problems that confront the minister in connection with housing.
First of all I think we have to recognize that the number of starts, the number of units that we have in the planning stage, the goal to which we are looking forward, has to be related to the economic impact this will have. It is impossible to isolate large housing programs from their economic impact on the Canadian economy. We are considering the problems of growth, we are considering replacements and then we are considering the number of people who actually need new houses. Immediately we are confronted, I believe, with a very serious problem. Are we going to build more units for living quarters at the expense of other economic expansion? Is it possible to get the maximum number of starts and still avoid an inflationary tendency, an increase in the money supply and the economic activity? These are I believe the real problems.
I do not believe we can isolate these economic impacts from a house building 
program. In so far as the planning of a city is concerned, I think we can give consideration to what has happened at Kitimat in British Columbia. The city of Kitimat was built by the Aluminum Company of Canada and planned as a city that would accommodate 50,000 people. If you want to study the housing problem in relation to the whole question of churches, schools, transportation, and so on, I think we have a good example in Kitimat. This is an example of what can be done when you are starting fresh. However, when we have a situation in which a good many people are involved, a lot of expropriation, transport problems, churches, schools, hospitals and so on, then you will not find a solution overnight.
So far as I am concerned these problems are not going to be solved by any stereotyped planning. I think we will find that every town, every area will have to be considered individually because of the climate, soil conditions and other factors such as railways, highways and so on. There are many factors that are going to be involved, so I do not believe we can entertain any stereotyped planning.
I suggest there are two things for which we are striving in connection with housing, and both have been mentioned here. Along with those who are getting new housing, we are also getting economic stimulation. Economic stimulation is there because you have various component parts such as the lumber industry, that is interested in the number of board feet going into any housing plan; the cement, hardware, heating and furnishings. The furnishings are a great part of the economic impact that goes along with any housing program.
I should like to draw attention to one very important point. I feel very strongly on this matter of interest rates. I think there ought to be a steady interest rate. If we are talking about a subsidy at all, I think this is the one place we should give consideration to a steady interest rate. We should give some consideration to what is happening in the United States. I think it is very unfortunate that one person entering into a contract today and another person entering into a contract two months from today should be paying a different percentage in interest. I think we should be giving serious consideration to the establishment of a revolving fund. This idea was advocated in 1954, I think it was, and was discussed before the banking and commerce committee in 1955. It was suggested at that time that a revolving fund be set up for housing and that the operation of this fund should determine the interest rate.

It was suggested at that time and, as I recall it, Graham Towers, the then governor of the Bank of Canada concurred in it, that an interest rate based on the revolving fund, or a service charge, could be more appropriately considered. This would be in the neighbourhood of 1J per cent to 2 per cent of the cost of the money supplied, and I believe this would be a step very much in the right direction and one which would decrease the over-all, long term cost of housing.
It would also have another effect, the effect of the impact on the economy of an extensive housing program. The extent by which we can reduce interest rates, thus reducing the over-all cost of a house after a 20 year period, will have an impact on the actual cost of the whole program, and we could give serious consideration to expanding the number of starts in our housing program without involving the expenditure of any more money. In my view this is important.
We shall have two or three questions to ask when we reach the committee stage, and so I shall conclude my remarks by saying I think the present minister is one in whom we have a great deal of confidence, and we are certainly looking forward to more action in connection with housing.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Chief Government Whip's assistant
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the National Housing Act implemented in 1954 has contributed to improve the standard of living of thousands of Canadians and it is essential to continue in that direction.
The government should be congratulated for making available to provinces and municipalities an amount of $100 million for urban redevelopment programs. Governments at every level are responsible for the carrying out of a co-ordinated and progressive slum clearance program implying at the same time a low cost housing program.
In Montreal, civic and provincial authorities, in co-operation with various associations, have designated as an historic district, the south central area of the city.
The new policy of the federal government authorizing loans for the renovation of existing homes will stimulate further the efforts of those who want to keep, as monuments, those old buildings full of souvenirs.
Other cities have already undertaken such a campaign to save our old buildings and they will extend to a greater number of property owners the benefits that C.M.H.C. makes available to them.
Another advantage of that measure is to allow those with modest means to acquire a house which has fallen into disrepair, to re-
National Housing Act
pair it out of the family budget, and to become the owner of an attractive home.
At the present time, it is easy to see that, in great cities, there are sections where houses are in such a poor condition that they look like slums and where living conditions are unacceptable. The new legislation will enable to check the extension of slums in the older sections of our cities. After restoration, these houses will enable low income families to obtain accommodation at a reasonable rent and enjoy the privilege of living in a clean and comfortable house.
I commend the government for the cooperation it wants to give the provinces in building homes for the aged or the people without a family, for its assistance to nonprofitable organizations in order to facilitate the building of houses for low income persons or families.
We appreciate the fact that the program of loans to universities will be continued since that will permit the construction of student residences.
Mr. Speaker, last November, the C.M.H.C. improved French Canadian representation within its ranks by changing the structure of its board and by increasing from four to six the number of its senior officials. Of the six executive directors, two are French Canadians, Messrs. Hector St-Pierre and Jean Paul Lupien. I hope the example set by C.M.H.C. will be followed by other crown corporations and federal departments. With a certain amount of goodwill, it is easy to give French Canadians a more equitable position within the federal civil service.
Anyone who goes over the reports of C.M.H.C. is bound to notice that Quebec does not participate in federal-provincial low rental housing projects. Between January 1, 1948 and October 31, 1962, out of a total 10,870 units built under that program, only 796 were erected in the province of Quebec, that is in the city of Montreal.
In Ontario, 37 municipalities benefited by that legislation. In Quebec, only Montreal took advantage of the program. Quebec municipalities and the provincial department of municipal affairs should co-ordinate their efforts and take full advantage of the National Housing Act in co-operation with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
It should be remembered that the National Housing Act authorizes the federal government to give financial help to any municipality which has, within its limits, areas where housing conditions can be improved. Through an agreement with a municipality and with the approval of the provincial government concerned, the federal government can contribute 75 per cent of the

National Housing Act
cost of an urban renewal study on the whole city and up to 50 per cent of the cost of a study on any particular area.
If, after those studies, it is decided that an area is in a state of advanced deterioration, the municipality can acquire the existing properties and clear the land for new residential or commercial construction.
The federal government will contribute 50 per cent of the cost of clearing and 75 per cent of the cost for new residential construction. The provincial government is called upon to take part in every agreement by means of a financial contribution and through the services of technicians of the department of municipal affairs. The Quebec minister of municipal affairs is to be commended for the initiative he took on May 27, when he created the "province of Quebec town planning award", to be given each year to the municipality submitting the best town planning program. Such a gesture should give new life to town planning.
Consultation between the town planning services of our municipalities, the municipal affairs department of each province and the directors of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will improve living conditions for a greater number of Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be very short but I have a different case to present than most other members. As everybody knows, a lot of potash developments are taking place at present in Saskatchewan, and although the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had given consideration to providing loans for housing where towns close to these potash mines needed them, nevertheless they have not gone as far in this direction as I and many others think desirable. I will mention, as an example, one town-the town of Lanigan. In Lanigan, or a few miles outside it, they are sinking a shaft and within a short time hundreds of people will be moving in. Before the potash mine comes into production new buildings and new houses will be going up-shops, businesses, schools, and so on. Later, hospitals will be required. But if these people cannot arrange a deal with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation we may run into a situation similar to that which developed in the town of Esterhazy where a potash mine is now in operation. This town grew by 150 per cent, if not 200 per cent after work on the sinking of the shaft was begun, but no co-ordinated planning was undertaken and virtually no houses were built by arrangement with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-although I must say the corporation is prepared to give the same deal to Lanigan as to larger cities.
[Mr. Rinfret.l
Nevertheless, the limitations when dealing with one-industry towns still exist, and the corporation can go no further.
I believe the provincial government will be visiting Ottawa again to discuss this problem with officials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. At the present time, as I say, they are doing as much as I suppose they are allowed to do under the existing regulations. The company itself is, probably, prepared to guarantee C.M.H.C. loans taken out by its own employees. But this town is concerned about those who are not employees of the company and who also have housing needs, and I should like the minister to assure us that consideration will be given to providing loans for business people and even municipalities in these circumstances. I should like the government to take another look at this situation together with the provincial government, and representatives of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in an effort to work out some suitable arrangement, because this is a serious matter. If we were only concerned with the situation during the sinking of the potash shaft, perhaps the situation would be tolerable; but we must think in terms of three or four years time, perhaps even less than that, when the mine comes into production and the need arises for many homes, additional business, hospitals, new schools and so forth. According to the planning done by the provincial government it is estimated that within six or eight years this town will grow to a population of approximately 8,000, as compared with the present population of 1,000. One can imagine what will happen if there are opportunities for these people to work, but no means by which they can obtain loans reasonably so as to build homes and put up all the other buildings which will be necessary. Lanigan could develop into a shacktown, if Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation do not change the regulation.
I am sure the departmental officials are familiar with this case because I have made representations more than once on this subject. I must say they were very co-operative and that they understood the situation very well. But they can only go as far as the act will allow. The government finds itself in a similar situation, I believe, at the present time. I was given to understand that in the very near future this question would be taken up again. I may say that there is more than one company involved. At the present time there are about 20 companies with interests in the province. The big future which lies ahead for potash means that more of these companies will be prepared to go ahead with plans for development. As a matter of fact,

I know of one company which had no intention of sinking a shaft until a short while ago. They have now made up their minds and they intend to sink a shaft, too. It will not be far away from Lanigan-one is to the east and the other is to the west.
So, without holding up proceedings any further, I should like to repeat that consideration has been given to these problems up to a certain point, but that the action taken has not gone as far as is desired and it would be most helpful to these small communities if more could be done. Should the minister need any additional information I am sure he will be able to obtain it from his officials because they are familiar with this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be happy to yield the floor if there is any agreement that the house should afterwards proceed to give second reading to this bill, but I understand there are to be other speakers and perhaps, in the circumstances, in view of the observations made by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, I might make some remarks on this subject.
This is indeed a piece of legislation with which, I am sure, everybody agrees. All I have heard so far are statements substantially in support of the bill. Statements have been made by spokesmen for the opposition to the effect that this is the kind of thing they had in mind. May I assure every member of the house that as a member of the mayors federation of Canada before I came to this place I recall appearing on several occasions over a period of three years before members of the cabinet to advocate legislation of this kind, not in its precise detail but as far as the broad principles are concerned. I think you will find, Mr. Speaker, that every mayor and every alderman of a municipality who has a genuine interest in the clearance of slums, in the prevention of the spread of blight and in the rebuilding of worn out downtown areas will be anxious for this house to proceed with the legislation now before us. It has been a long awaited and urgently needed measure. At the municipal level of government it will assist them to do the job they wish to accomplish, in co-operation with the national government and the federal government, so as
National Housing Act
to bring about a betterment of social conditions in the housing field. They want to make a contribution to the economic health of Canada by redeveloping blighted and worn out commercial areas.
We all see a new opportunity for employment in the capital goods sector of our economy. We find an opportunity here, while engaging in a social act, to provide employment for people in the building trades, both on the site and off the site, in the plants which produce building materials throughout the entire region of Canada. We also want to prepare for what everyone tells us is an increasing density of population in the urban areas of Canada. If the prognostications of our economists are correct, we will need this kind of urban renewal program on its way as rapidly as possible, because they tell us-I think they are substantially in agreement and I do not think anybody challenges this kind of economic thought-that more and more people in this world are finding a need to locate jobs and positions in the servicing sector of the economy, as compared with the productive side of economic activity, due first of all to population growth and second to the fact of automation in industry. So it is an inescapable fact that around the urban areas you will find continuing the oft described population explosion.
The bill attempts to make its contribution to the desires of the municipalities and the provinces by rewording the provisions of the act which have to do with the areas in which the federal government, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, may participate. In the previous statute, as I understand it, there was some restriction with regard to the kind of area in which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could participate. I refer to that particular section which required that there be a substantial quantity of housing. I believe the present proposal will remove that particular restrictive clause. While it requires comprehensive planning, I believe it will remove that particular clause and enable the clearance of blighted commercial districts as well as blighted slum areas. This would be a great encouragement to those at the municipal level of government who found from their planning advisers that you could not hope to accomplish a good urban renewal program if you confined yourself to a very narrow block of clearance, and it would require a much more expanded area if you wished to encourage redevelopment in the region of residential as well as commercial redevelopment.
Then the proposal to assist financially the municipalities in providing the capital for their share of the programs in the field of urban renewal will also be welcomed. But the

National Housing Act
act, if you read it carefully, as it did before, attempts to encourage what is called comprehensive planning. What this means really is that the Canadian government, in giving assistance to municipalities through and with the co-operation of the provinces, want to be sure that the end objectives will be reached, and when we talk about the need for comprehensive planning in an act of this kind we are referring to proper land use plans, which are the product of some very serious and extensive planning by competent planning authorities. It means the existence of legislation which compels the observance of minimum standards. It certainly requires housing outside the area projected for redevelopment being subjected to examination to make sure that the blighted conditions will not develop outside the area being redeveloped. This requires a very rigid application of minimum standard laws at the municipal level of government. It also requires, in this field of so-called comprehensive planning, some very informed and extensive studies of the economic base from which the region derives its growth and development. Without that knowledge you might very well undertake a clearance program and then find land which you have cleared lying undeveloped for some years to come.
This observation of mine derives from a comment made by one hon. member this afternoon who was talking about the need for a ministry of housing. If he meant by this that we need to increase our interest in this field under whatever minister it may come, I heartily agree. As a matter of fact, comprehensive planning for a city requires a knowledge and understanding of the economics of the region in which it is located, and it requires some comprehensive planning of the entire region around it. This brings you into an understanding of what is the comprehensive planning of the ARDA program to be, and how it relates to developments within urban areas. I suggest that the two fields of activity, at least with respect to general, overall planning of land usage, are involved with the same kind of problem. So if we pass this legislation, the municipalities will have the challenge back in their hands to attack the bad social conditions of bad housing; to meet the challenge of helping to provide employment in the capital goods sector by redevelopment; and they will have to meet the challenge of preparing for the future growth and development of their urban areas by virtue of a population explosion which will continue because of the economic realities of our time.
Some reference was made by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) to the need

for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation activities being expanded in the northern parts of Canada. I think this is a separate problem. Here the hon. member is talking about the need for government policy in urging, assisting and encouraging proper housing development in those great northern areas. This is really what you might call new development as distinct from redevelopment. There is no question that this requires the attention of government. However, I was pleased to find a member of the opposition appealing to the minister to give his attention to it, because no doubt he made the same appeal to the government he supported in the past few years, and had failed to achieve any success in this regard. Now he turns to the new minister and hopes this government will achieve the success which his government failed to obtain previously. In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I welcome his observation. I think I can assure him that this government will co-operate in reaching the objectives and solutions which he says are so badly needed.
Some reference was made by another hon. member to giving credit to Winnipeg for leading the way. I think I would be remiss in my duty, representing the constituency of Halifax, if I did not draw attention to the fact that in 1957 we began with a program, 75 per cent financed by the federal government, to make a study of the Halifax region. Then came a major clearance project; this was followed by building some 340 units and rehousing displaced people, and this was followed by development proposals being called for, not only from Canada but throughout the world. Then only a few weeks ago did we have an agreement signed for a redevelopment project amounting to some $35 million of new commercial and housing construction in that older city of Canada. In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say that Halifax is in the vanguard in this connection, and received in this respect the cooperation of the former government and the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) who is sitting opposite. I am sure that the government which is now in office will extend the same co-operation to all areas which have comprehensive plans and which have real, genuine needs to be met. I am sure such areas will receive the co-operation of this government to at least an equal degree, if not to a greater degree, than that accorded those seeking it on previous occasions.

In an era of inflation and high
National Housing Act
taxation I think consideration should be given to this particular suggestion so that these people will be in a better economic position, because they are the ones who spend the money and who keep our economy rolling. subtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASED EXEMPTION IN NORTHERN AREAS
SUGGESTED INCREASED EXEMPTION IN NORTHERN AREAS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so that Canadian taxpayers residing in the high-cost northerly areas of Canada be allowed an increased personal exemption to that now allowed under the Income Tax Act in order to:
(1)	encourage and accelerate population growth in Canada's northern areas;
(2)	assist in creating a permanent population in Canada's north;
(3)	remove the discriminatory tax burden which now exists as between the northern Canadian taxpayer and those taxpayers living in the more southerly areas of Canada; and
(4)	eliminate the hardship now caused to families in the lower income group now residing, and to reside, in Canada's northern areas.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it will probably come as no surprise to hon. members to learn that the subject matter of this resolution was considered by treasury board in 1955, 1956 and 1957 during the last years of the Liberal government of that time. The evidence indicating this emerged in the discussions of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters in 1959, I believe.
The resolution is based on four premises: First, that it is desirable to encourage population growth in that 40 per cent of Canada lying above the 60th parallel and, indeed, the northerly portions of the provinces of Canada; second, that it is desirable as a principle to create a permanent population in Canada's northland as opposed to accepting the transitory growth to which the north has been subjected over the years; third, that there does exist discrimination in the tax burden which is now borne by residents of southern Canada compared with that borne by those who live in the more northerly areas of Canada; fourth, that there is recognition

that there does exist hardship with respect to families in the lower income group who reside in Canada's north.
When I spoke earlier this afternoon I had occasion to refer to the higher costs of construction. Where a home can be constructed for $10,000 in the more southerly centres of Canada, that same home will cost $14,000 in the more northerly areas of Canada above the 60th parallel. Food costs in northern Canada, expressed in terms of percentage, are some 27 per cent higher than they are in the more southerly areas of Canada.
The government itself recognizes that it does cost more to live in Canada's north because several years ago they established the principle of compensating civil servants for the loss of wages that would occur by reason of the higher cost of living in the northerly areas as a result of their being required to move there. If a Department of Transport employee, an employee of the Department of National Defence or, indeed, an employee of any department of the government was required to move from say Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto or some other city to Whitehorse, Dawson City, Yellowknife, Inuvik or Alert, the government recognized that it would cost that civil servant more to live in those northerly areas. Therefore the government implemented a system of compensation known as isolated post allowances, which is still in existence.
Isolated post allowances are based on the assessment of four basic living factors as opposed to living in the southerly areas of Canada. The government takes into account the difference in cost of heating and lighting in the north as opposed to southern centres. The government also takes into consideration when paying these allowances the difference in the cost of food. This is a separate factor. In paying these isolated post allowances the government also takes into account factors of isolation, such as whether or not there are those social amenities available in the north as are available in the more southerly areas of Canada.
Upon these factors various positions in the north are graded, and in the case of a married man a maximum of $2,600 over and above his basic pay and allowances as a civil servant is paid to the civil servant who is posted to the north. Mind you, that civil servant still pays income tax on his isolated post allowance, and this has been a matter of complaint on the part of the civil servant for several years. On the one hand, the government pays him an allowance to compensate him for the difference in the cost of living in the north and, on the other hand, takes it away in the form of income tax. It has been argued, and supported by several

public organizations in the north, that the same principle should be applied not only to civil servants who live in the northerly areas of Canada but also to other Canadians, because those other Canadians who are carrying out jobs on all fours with those of civil servants in the north are subjected to the same increased costs of living as the civil servant.
If the government recognizes the principle of paying isolation allowances to civil servants in the north, I suggest there is a good deal of merit to the argument that the same principle should be applied to all Canadians who live in northern Canada. Otherwise, instead of encouraging a permanent population growth, which in turn would stabilize the economy of northern Canada, a desirable objective, what we have is a transitory population, people who go to the north for a year or two years, perhaps longer but not much, and who then move away because they find they cannot cope with the increased cost of living. Only those members of the northern communities who are in the middle or upper income brackets find it comfortable to live in Canada's north.
This is one of the reasons why I suggested to the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) that in revising the National Housing Act specific attention should be paid to existing northern conditions which prohibit buildings of a standard comparable to those in southern areas. Because of the pioneer and undeveloped nature of Canada's north it is essential that the government consider all national legislation in the light of northern conditions.
There are those who will say that the Income Taxt Act is a national act and therefore must have national application. Those who say this will put forward the view that if an increased personal income tax exemption is granted to northern residents justification can also be found to apply the same tax alleviation to people in Newfoundland and the maritimes, because their individual income earning capacity is less than that of people in Ontario. In the light of the greater unemployment in the province of Quebec, I suppose the same argument can be said to apply particularly there.
But this resolution is based fundamentally on the premise that it is desirable to develop Canada's northland so that it can make its full contribution toward national development. There are many today who took upon Canada's north in the same light as the opponents of the construction of the railroad to the west coast looked upon the western part of this country at that time. My friend, the member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) mentions Great Slave lake.
I can recall the vote in this house at that time
Income Tax Act
when those who now sit on the government side voted against the construction of that railway.
Then, I saw a very interesting article in the Montreal Gazette reporting on a meeting the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) addressed in Vancouver, a meeting of the Vancouver chamber of commerce, which indicated that the minister, at least as one occupant of the government benches, had caught the vision. He has caught something of the vision that had been so much ridiculed and derided by members on that side when they were in opposition. According to this newspaper article the minister had caught a vision which they described as a booming vision, which is indeed encouraging, particularly in the light of the vote on the Pine Point railroad, which hon. members did not seem to think was a good idea, and in the light of a certain pattern that seems to be emerging so far as northern development is concerned, since this government has been in office.
I will be quite candid and say that I endeavoured, as the committee will show, to have this matter reconsidered by treasury board, at the time the standing committee on mines, forests and waters was sitting in 1958-59. However, I did not receive too much encouragement at that time. I am hoping that if the minister has really caught the vision, as I think he would like to do-but I feel he is prevented from doing so by his colleagues in the cabinet-then I can count on him for support. I see his parliamentary secretary is in his seat, and I hope he will participate in this debate in support of this motion. I can inform the parliamentary secretary, as I am sure he knows after travelling in the north, this motion is supported by every northern resident. They are up there as the caretakers for Canada, the caretakers for 40 per cent of Canada, and if the proper approach is used this northern part of the country will make a substantial contribution to national growth.
One way in which we can encourage the growth and development of that part of the country is to adopt a policy for attracting people. The potential is there. The mining potential is there, and I do not think anybody will disagree with that, least of all the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources or anyone else associated with him in his department. Certainly he is selling this idea of northern development to private investment, but the government has a part to play. We had a policy when this party was in office, a policy of partnership, whereby government and private industry worked hand in hand in the development of the Canadian north. A pattern seems to be

Income Tax Act
emerging now, and the position is that private enterprise seems to have the major part of the responsibility. Being a northener, I am of the positive opinion that government has a very definite part to play in the building of the north, and that is to create an atmosphere which will attract investment.
The manner in which the government creates that atmosphere is subject to varying points of view. I feel that the program which was followed by this party when it held office proved that long range programs for the establishment of communications, the construction of highways and the like, will assist in creating an atmosphere that will attract the necessary investment to open northern Canada. One of the best methods for attracting that investment and creating the atmosphere which will be conducive to the permanent development of the north is to make it a desirable place in which to live, to equalize the cost of living in the north with the cost of living in similar southerly areas. We do not have all the social amenities that exist in Ottawa, Vancouver and Winnipeg. These differences can be borne by the northern resident if his living conditions are reasonably comfortable and if he knows that the contribution he is making as a pioneer is being appreciated by the rest of Canada, and particularly by the government.
One of the methods which I suggest in the resolution is to equalize the tax treatment of northern residents. As I have said, treasury board refused to give such serious consideration to northern areas. However, the merits of this resolution indicate it is something that just cannot be sloughed off by the house or by the government. It may be that the government and the house are not prepared to accept this resolution and I have every reason to expect it will be talked out tonight. Perhaps there is justification for this, because it is something the house cannot accept within the space of one hour. I suggest to the government however that they resubmit the merits of this resolution to the treasury board in the light of the remarks made here and in the committee as well. I suggest they assess it in the light of the remarks that have been made in the various sessions of the Yukon legislative council and, although I have not checked them I am sure my hon. friend will, in the light of the remarks that have been made in the council of the Northwest Territories. I hope the parliamentary secretary to the minister will speak on the motion and give some indication of the government's feeling. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will speak as well. I should like to hear from my friend, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories. I do not want

to occupy more of the time of the house, so I would commend to the house the merits of the resolution in the hope the government will see its way clear to investigate fully the suggestions set forth in the resolution.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? I notice that he suggests as one of the purposes of the resolution the elimination of hardships, for families of lower income groups. I should like to ask him whether or not the increasing of the exemption for personal income tax in the north would be of any help to the great majority of people in the north, the Eskimos and Indians, who are not earning sufficient money to come within the income tax provisions?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASED EXEMPTION IN NORTHERN AREAS

Well, this gets to the root of the formula which would accomplish the objective set forth in the resolution. Within the limits of his understanding he has come up with a suggestion that may provide some answers. I am trying to help the hon. member perform his job a little better by pointing out to him that there is certainly nothing wrong with suggesting that people who find an opportunity in Canada's north to develop a resource will certainly examine the economics of the development before investing their private capital, and will find they must pay incentives to attract skilled workers to the region. You will find that the operator who knows what he is doing will attempt to fix his salary rates at a point where, after income tax, they will be attractive to the kind of skills he wants in that region.
There may be exceptions to this general rule, but generally speaking, if we have any kind of good common sense in the management of the private enterprise sector of our economy, the end result is bound to be that wage and salary levels will be fixed at that point where the private entrepreneur calculates he can induce the skills he requires for his particular undertaking in the north region.
I have no quarrel with the hon. member when he suggests that civil servants who are faced with additional costs in the north, and with expenses which they would not normally meet in the developed central and southern parts of Canada, should be adequately compensated to put them into a position of equivalence with their fellow civil servants in the particular department in which they happen to be engaged. There is no quarrel with that; but I think you can accomplish more for the development of the resources of the north in other ways, and;

Income Tax Act
with much more adequate tools of government at your command, tools that can be employed to accomplish these objectives.
We are learning much about the economic bases of regions. Only today we were discussing the matter of urban renewal. You cannot have good urban renewal development unless you undertake some practical studies of the economic base of the blighted region which you are redeveloping, and the same thing is true of the northern sectors of this country.
Preceding development, there must be economic feasibility to the development of a resource, and you must be able to demonstrate this to investors, whether it be investors from government in the field of social capital, or whether it be private entrepreneurs who invest their money and take the risks. This means a pretty extensive and well developed examination of a resource in a practical way, if one hopes to encourage and accelerate population growth in Canada's northern areas. You just do not put people there and then keep them there. There must be opportunities for work and employment.
