Besides, I am only a backbencher. When you get down to the benches in front, there are men of great experience and ability to whom the hon. member can make his plea.
I understand the research staff of the royal commission is now examining this question and it is possible that the commission in its report will deal with the subject. I have no indication of the views of the commission, but I am informed that some former ministers of finance were not convinced of the efficacy of this proposal. This motion seems to assume that a person residing in northern Canada is at the present time being discriminated against under the income tax law as compared with a person living in southern Canada. He bases this on the assertion that a resident of northern Canada must incur higher costs which are not recognized by the income tax legislation. This would seem to suggest that personal exemptions under the Income Tax Act be directly related to some basic cost of living index, and increased where costs exceed a certain basic amount. I think this is the idea the hon. member was struggling with. If this were done, it would follow in logic and in equity that exemptions should be increased not only with respect to such high cost areas as there may be in the north but also with respect to high cost areas elsewhere in Canada, such as the larger metropolitan areas. There is certainly a notable differential in school teachers salaries in metropolitan areas as compared with areas outside. May I say that anybody who has served on a city council and who has dealt with tax matters knows there is a vast differential between salaries paid in metropolitan areas as compared with those outside the borders.
Presumably the exemptions would have to be established annually as a result of cost of living studies. Such a change would create anomalies which would bring the tax system into disrepute, cause confusion to taxpayers and tax collectors alike, and result in a significant reduction in revenue. If you need the revenue, then obviously if you forgo it in one place you have to find it somewhere else. Nowhere in the statement made by the hon. member was any suggestion made as to how the lost revenue would be made up, unless he thought that with the development of our northern resources there would be sufficient yield to the Canadian economy to make it worth while. If that is what he had in mind, I think he should have said so. But the hon.

member certainly did not say so in the course of his observations on the resolution. If the principle of relating the personal exemptions to the cost of living in particular areas were adopted and followed to its logical conclusion it might be reasonable to lower the exemptions for taxpayers who resided in low cost areas. I am sure most hon. members know from experience that some of these low cost areas are not at all remote from municipalities in which living costs are quite high. It seems to me that to allow different exemption levels to taxpayers in the same province, or indeed in the same country would be completely unacceptable, yet such a system would be almost inevitable if personal exemptions were tied to area living costs.
The motion alleges that the additional allowance would eliminate the hardship caused to families in the lower income group now residing in Canada's northern areas. I suggest that it would not have this result and, in fact, by increasing the disposable incomes of the taxpayers in the higher income brackets it might eventually drive prices higher, thus penalizing their less fortunate neighbours. Even if the change suggested in the motion could be confined to certain defined high-cost northern areas it would be of no help to people in the very low income groups, because they are not taxable.

There are, without doubt, some forms of relief which are given to the people in the northerly areas of the provinces. Consideration is being given, and I hope it will result in something being done in this respect, to the question of petroleum products. I would hope that the equalization of the cost of petroleum products, gasoline, fuel oil, and

so on, would be a reality in British Columbia within a matter of a year or two. speechtext:
The first important reason, I think, was touched on by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) when he said the government has implemented a special program of allowances for federal officers in the Canadian north. This allowance gives upwards of $2,100 a year in addition to basic salary. The northern allowance, as it has come to be called in the country, is received monthly as a part of the pay cheque of federal government employees. They pay income tax on it, but that particular additional bonus is a recognition of higher costs in that part of the country. I can recall a few years back when I lived in the far north, around the mouth of the Mackenzie river, that it was not unusual for an individual to have to pay a fuel bill of $100 a month during the winter months for fuel oil. It is not an exaggeration to say that electricity may cost a private individual $50 or $60 a month during the dark days of the winter. Food prices were out of this world, to the extent that anyone not in the employ of the federal service just went without. I can recall talking to employees whose families had not had any eggs, apples, oranges, lettuce, tomatoes or fresh foods of any kind for well over 18 months, because apples were $3 a dozen, so were oranges, and fresh eggs were $1.65 a dozen. These are the facts of life, as any northerner will tell you. Any real northerner will not be put off by such statements as: "If you live in Toronto you have extra expenses too". I guarantee
Income Tax Act
that that sort of thing will not only be rejected out of hand by true northerners, but it will also do the minister of northern affairs no good when I mail copies of Hansard to every person in the north.
The northern allowance does have quite serious drawbacks. It drives a wedge between federal government employees who are in receipt of it and others who are not. It is a critical issue because there is a growing rift between federal civil servants and those who are not federal civil servants, which is always the case whenever there are special benefits to civil servants which are not general throughout the whole populace. This, of course, is a completely arbitrary administrative decision. In some communities northern allowance was decreased. In some cases the employees were advised at the beginning of the month that the allowance would be reduced, and some employees lost $40 a month, with absolutely no recourse open to them. As I say, this is an administrative decision which was taken in an arbitrary manner and without consultation. Salaries in some cases were reduced by as much as $360 a year to $480 a year. This allowance, which recognizes the high cost of living in the north, was reduced without consultation, and from the point of view of the civil servants themselves they would prefer that their salary be not subject to revision or to the whimsical dictates of a government which is attempting to prune its costs. You could eliminate the northern allowance by allowing an increased personal exemption, with a 25 per cent cut in taxes across the board.
The suggestion which was made earlier today by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd) I feel cannot be taken too seriously, and I do not think it was meant to be anything more than a time waster. There are ample precedents for the provision of special incentives for undeveloped areas. For example, one need only consider what happened in western Canada a few years ago when the federal government encouraged people to settle and to set up homesteads. For as little as $5 rent 160 acres was provided, and this proved to be a way to open up the country.
Another important reason why this resolution should be approved borders on a highly dangerous area of discussion. As the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) suggested, many of the residents of the north are not taxpayers at all. For example, the Indian and Eskimo people do not earn enough to pay taxes. These are the people who require most of the services which are supported by taxation. There is a small minority of people in the north, who tend to be among the non-Eskimo and non-Indian group, who pay most of the taxes. They are

Income Tax Act
such people as small businessmen, workers in the mines, successful trappers and fishermen. The civil servants are compensated through payment of northern allowance, but I would suggest that tax relief is absolutely essential if people are to remain in that part of the country. This resolution has suggested one compensation could be effected by increasing personal exemptions. I suggest it would be equally easy merely to allow people in the Canadian north-the Yukon and Northwest Territories-to compute their taxes using the same schedules and forms used by anyone else in Canada, and then having arrived at the computation of tax payable, deduct 25 per cent as bonus for having the courage to go into Canada's hinterland and help develop it. I reject the suggestion that would have to be done elsewhere. There are elsewhere provincial governments with various forms of tax relief which they can make available. In the Northwest Territories and the Yukon the federal government still carries the bulk of the investment and bears the bulk of the responsibility for developing those areas intelligently.
In conclusion, and to allow the house time to approve this resolution, I want to suggest to the government, though I realize they cannot pass the resolution, not just to reject it but to refer it to treasury board. There is general support for this measure in the Canadian north. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources knows this is true. This would be a generally accepted measure in the north which would bring a great deal of relief to the people there. It is a measure which has been sought for many years, and it might even rewin a seat for the Liberal party at the next election.

In the few minutes allowed to me this evening I should like to say that the reason we cannot accept this resolution in its present form is that, although its prime purpose is to eliminate hardship among the lower income groups in the north, its effect would be the contrary because it would benefit only those people in the north who are already

within the income tax brackets. To increase personal exemptions would mean that those people in the higher income groups would also have an increased personal exemption, which would be of no benefit at all to thousands of northerners, particularly the Eskimos and Indians, who do not come within the ambit of the Income Tax Act because they do not earn enough money.
In terms of incentive, the incentive we should be looking for is the incentive to bring about industry in the north, to provide more employment for the people there. We should provide capital investment stimulus, a write-off in the case of new mineral and petroleum industries, equalization of transportation costs, and equalization of certain freight rates. That is the type of thing which would do much to equalize the cost of living in the north, rather than raising the personal exemption of those people now living in the north.

May I reiterate that I am quite sure this bill will receive rather speedy consideration by the house, so the minister may be at his ease and not be concerned about the few brief interventions that will be made this evening. I note that so far 28 government measures have been adopted. I think we are doing very well in the house, and this measure will receive the same approval.
With regard to the application of mortgage funds to older homes, 1 think the minister has made a very notable step in the right direction, but I think the approach is wrong in that this provision will apply only in designated areas and where the federal, provincial and municipal governments have entered into an agreement. I recognize readily the reason for moving in this way and I think everyone on this side of the house recognizes this point. Had such action been taken many years ago prior to the rapid urban growth following world war II, I believe many of the situations that have arisen would not have occurred. For instance, there was the great sprawl of the urban areas away from the central concentrations of population, which created educational and commercial problems, and the housing problem, of course, with all its complexities so far as municipal services are concerned and other matters pertaining to this growth. I feel that some of the areas that will now be affected by this provision would have maintained their position. I think that money would have been spent to maintain and improve them and therefore, so far as the taxpayers are concerned, the cost would not have been so great.
But let us move on to the situation as it is today. As I said this afternoon, certainly I was aware of the problem when we on this side formed the government, and I did make representations in this regard at that time. But that does not stop me from expressing myself this evening and endeavouring to impress the minister. Many older homes in smaller municipalities and towns would benefit if this measure applied, but the thinking, of course, involves a much different type of area. In other words, an area within a large urban centre has to be 20220-258
National Housing Act
designated a slum area before the amendment to the act can be applied. As I say, the minister is certainly moving in the right direction, but in making this change he has not in my opinion gone far enough. I know that not only my own home town, which is small in relation to the areas he is thinking of in this regard, but hundreds of others would benefit greatly if this provision covered them.
I am thinking this evening of the working people of the country who could have taken advantage of this provision in a most beneficial way, but who have availed themselves already of the opportunity to build new homes. In my view this has not provided the greatest benefit to the economy because some of these people have had to jeopardize a great many years of their lives in order to carry the charges that go along with the construction of these new homes under the terms available to these people.
I also mentioned this afternoon the matter of tax abatement. I will include that in my summary, but at this time I will move along to another phase of the legislation which I think is also very good and which we will probably find satisfactory when the minister explains it. I refer to the new section 36B where reference is made to the acquisition of existing buildings in order to convert them for school or university uses. I have discussed a specific problem with the minister and I believe this particular section will apply. I am sure it will be a very valuable measure in this regard.
With the rising costs of education and the increasing demand for higher education, universities and their boards in most cases find themselves in difficult circumstances in fulfilling the programs they have laid out for themselves and meeting the goals which must be attained in order to keep pace with the educational requirements not only of today but of the future. As the directors of these universities plan their program for the coming years, I hope the minister will see fit to expand the application of this section respecting the acquisition of property, because in many cases property that is available today will not be available five or ten years hence at which time the property, if acquired now, will be very valuable to the functioning of these institutions. As the clause is framed I think it will probably meet this situation, but I think it should be clarified in the minister's own words.
Then, the situation to which I have made reference involves a national housing subdivision of some years ago, and I think the disposition of this land by the corporation will be entertained in the not too distant

National Housing Act
future. Where such circumstances exist, I think it would be wise for the minister to go on record and say that such an institution of learning will have priority for the acquisition of this land and the buildings existing thereon.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to present a brief summary of my points before I resume my seat. I would say this:
1.	The loans for the purchase of older homes should have general application rather than the specific application referred to in the amendment.
2.	The interest on the mortgages should be allowed as a reduction from taxable income. I should like to add a word here. We are well aware, as I am sure the minister is, of the application of recent legislation in the United States. It is generally on a much broader base than I suggested here, but certainly we must start somewhere. In this regard, I am making this recommendation to the minister because of the situation I outlined with regard to the worker who has to prejudice his income position for so many years to purchase a home and who, we all consider, is the backbone of the Canadian economy. We must do everything in our power to keep that man in a strong and flexible position. This is one area in which the federal government could make a valuable contribution by following my suggestion.
3.	I should like the minister to explain, perhaps not now but when we get into committee, the situation with regard to section 36(b).
4.	I would recommend to the government the establishment of a department of urban growth and development for the benefit of the planning of communities such as the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) referred to earlier today. I believe that in a country such as ours, with the potential growth we have, with the great wealth we have and the future everyone knows stands before us, we should be prepared to do everything in our power to see that this growth is established on a proper basis for the citizens of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
In introducing this legislation the minister indicated that it represented a substantial shift in the philosophy of the legislation, and in its emphasis, by the program which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as the instrument of government, will be undertaking in the period ahead. I am sure that people who review this period, in writing the history of social legislation and social development, will mark this series of amendments to the housing act as one of the most significant developments in terms of the obligation that
[Mr. Winkler.)
lies upon us today. So far, as the minister pointed out very well, the emphasis has been on new, single family housing built in the suburbs to satisfy the immediate demand for housing accommodation, which has been accumulated as a result of a long period of under construction, and to compensate for the new family formations that have taken place.
This phase, which has occupied something like 90 per cent of the units constructed so far, is coming to an end. The emphasis is now shifting to urban renewal and public housing, and properly so. As the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) said this afternoon, there is no greater challenge ahead for any government or for any party than to meet the problem of the development of our cities and the redevelopment of the core of the cities, and to provide a proper balance of the required housing accommodation for different types of families in our society. The people who did the forecasts of population trends for the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects indicated that in something like two decades approximately 80 per cent of our population will be living in a fairly small number of large metropolitan centres. This is just one way of expressing what the obligation is.
We are now beginning to see the consequences of this tremendous overemphasis on single family accommodation, the three bedroom bungalow in the suburbs. One result has been the creation of some very fine, attractive new suburbs. This is where our children are being born and a large part of our population is being reared. However, the suburban communities which have been built this way do not have an adequate cross-section of the population. There has been a tremendous demand in these communities, for example, for schools. I predict that this demand is in excess of the long term requirements of many of these areas. This, in turn, comes back to the defect in the legislation, which should have placed a proper emphasis on multiple; accommodation and proper emphasis on public housing in particular, which is needed.
These amendments mark a milestone in the development of our philosophy in terms of what our legislation is devised to do. We all know that in this country a matter like housing, as the minister so well indicated, involves a co-operative partnership of municipal, provincial and federal authorities working together to solve a problem which must, in the first instance, be initiated at the municipal level. There is, as other members who participated in the debate before me have indicated, a reluctance, which is frequently difficult to understand, by the municipal authorities to initiate public housing

projects. There are many reasons for this. In many instances, the starts that have been made have not been as good as they should have been.
Some of the starts on public housing, and I am referring to the city of Ottawa, have been made without adequate planning of recreational areas adjacent to the public housing. Some of the projects that have been undertaken have not been properly inspected in the course of construction, so the standards of construction dropped. The accommodation which now exists is not as good as it should be. These are technical defects which we can remedy as we go along.
The important thing at this stage is to set the legislation in perspective to create the initiatives to do the things that have to be done. There is an obligation on the municipal authorities at every stage, as the minister indicated. There is the problem of acquiring land, the problem of the rehabilitation of existing housing, the conservation of housing before it deteriorates beyond hope.
The legislation and the amendments are specifically directed towards the older housing within the designated urban renewal areas. The corporation is now permitted to participate in the cost, not only of acquiring the land but the actual replanning of the services that have to go with the land. Frequently, the services have to be improved in order to meet the new demands placed upon them. The sewer mains and water mains have to meet the demands of the use of the land after redevelopment.
The municipalities must show initiative. They must go ahead with legislation to create housing standards boards and to set up standards for the maintenance of existing housing, and procedures for the condemning of housing which is below standard. The province is usually ready to contribute by providing a legislative base to back up the municipalities, so that this type of legislation does not become challenged in the courts. I was pleased to note, Mr. Speaker, that the city of Ottawa, which has pioneered a piece of legislation, was upheld in the Supreme Court of Canada. This legislation permitted the municipality to levy a high rise charge on new buildings in older areas which would create new demands on services which are inadequate to sustain them, when the tenements in the older areas constructed half a century ago are replaced by high rise buildings. The sewers that were laid down 50 years ago are not adequate; the water mains which were laid down 50 years ago are not giving sufficient pressure. The services which are below ground, in addition to the services above ground, have to be replaced.
20220-258i
National Housing Act
For the first time the legislation will now permit Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to participate in the costs of redevelopment, but the municipality has a responsibility-as I think the city of Ottawa has obviously done, and as a result of which other municipalities will follow-to seek the sources of revenue that are adequate to participate in the opportunities now offered it.
We heard some very interesting comments from the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) in terms of guidance, what might be short term and what might be long term policy. I for one followed his comments with a great deal of interest. There were some assertions he made with which I could agree, but there were other comments which he made that I found a little bit academic and on the theoretical side, with which I could not agree.
I would like to make some comments on one aspect of the bill which is not covered in the amendment, but which I am sure will be reviewed in years ahead. I am thinking in terms of land assembly projects. The hon. member said such a project was a very good example of the type of difficulty in basic thinking, and in trying to decide what our objectives should be. If we are shifting our emphasis to multiple units or public housing, to me it is quite clear that public housing should be built first in land assembly projects.
If we permit a land assembly project to be sold off in lots at a subsidized rate to a number of buyers in the middle income bracket, the experience all too frequently has been that the purchasers come back and lobby against public housing being built on land assembly projects. The people who buy these sites are under a misunderstanding as to what public housing involves. I believe there is an obligation to put the priority first on the building of public housing sites, and then sell the rest of the land assembly project sites for single family homes to private purchasers.
As an observer of some of the land assembly projects I could not help but notice that there is perhaps a real question whether the objectives of good, low cost, economical housing are achieved. It is clear now that the industry is moving to larger and larger units of production. A builder who puts up fewer than 100 units a year is not able to take advantage of the economics of large scale purchasing, and when you take a land assembly project and make it available to individual purchasers they in turn negotiate with a wide range of builders, and this means we have an uneconomical type of operation involved. More and more the industry today calls for plans not to put up a

National Housing Act
single home but a neighbourhood of homes, a cluster of homes, harmonious in design, to give a balanced neighbourhood and a balanced community.
In making the sites available from the land assembly projects I submit it is very much in the public interest that we should look in terms of the number of builders who are going to operate there, and make restrictions to ensure that the finest type of neighbourhood development takes place within our land assembly schemes.
One other concept advanced by the hon. member for Danforth gave me a fair amount of concern. He spoke in terms of a model community. This is the great dream of the past. In the model community everything is ordered, everything is according to plan, but you will find very few of those who have had practical experience with the industry who feel that this type of community can be created in the way the planners think it can.
What is going to be the core of the community? If it is industry, how are you going to have public control of the industry? In a socialist economy it would be possible to formulate policy so that you could direct this core and work out from the industrial locations to the residential sections, and thus achieve a balance; but in our society it would be very doubtful if you could do this.
Was the hon. member thinking in terms of industrial communities on the fringe of large residential areas? If so, he must think in terms of what is involved, how many builders are going to be involved; because if it is open to everyone, this is to the detriment of the land assembly project. If you restrict the number of builders, by what principles do you allocate the lots and erect the homes? How do you assign plots of serviced land and put on the type of controls which are flexible enough and yet sufficiently minimum to be adequate?
I believe we are now entering a phase in construction in North America, and in Canada in particular, in which private industry is rising to a high level of achievement. I think the satellite communities which we now see springing up are the best planned towns, the kind we now see rising in southern Ontario, on the outskirts of Toronto, and which we see planned on the outer fringe of the green belt beyond Ottawa. In many cases a single large developer, or combination of developers, has reached to the satellite community, and set up within the framework of private enterprise its own controls, its own planning, and its own objectives.
I do not think this calls for anything more than proper balance and the guidance of legislation, but one of the things which has

been involved so much with our legislation so far has been this monstrosity of emphasis on the three bedroom, single family bungalow in the suburbs. This has distorted the community's attractiveness and has created onerous and unnecessary demands on school boards and others. It has created what I think in many cases is an unequal disposition of new classrooms and other new facilities, especially when we come to add up the cost of this type of inadequate planning.
I think the amendments which have been proposed today are a stepping stone in a change of thinking, in a change of philosophy, in a change of emphasis which is in keeping with the obligations ahead of us. There is no question that the greatest job to be done in housing today is to provide houses for those in the lower income brackets, to provide housing on the most economical terms, whether it be in forms of town houses, apartment dwellings or multiple units which are beautiful, which are economical, which provide the necessary minimum standards of community facilities and which, I submit, will have to be financed with the kind of assistance which single family homes got through the previous legislation. I am very pleased to welcome these amendments and to support them in this house.

I welcome the hon. member's intervention, and I am delighted to say I can vouch for the fact that the hon. member who has spoken is an excellent citizen and a well known resident of a very fine riding. The hon. member was attentive to what I was saying and I am sure he will recall I said there were some instances of standards of construction which are not as good as they should be, and I also referred to lack of adequate balance, of recreational facilities and lands adjacent to public housing sites. I feel very strongly that this is one particular example where the planning was not good enough, and I believe that what we will have to do in future will have to be a great deal better than was done there. But by the same token we all know we have to have public

housing. This is what is needed, and this is what is called for within the terms of public initiative.
We have, by and large, solved the problem of the development of the single family house. Eighty per cent of what has been done under the act has concerned this type of accommodation. But I have worked very conscientiously to try to improve the conditions of that development, and as an alderman of the city of Ottawa representing that area I have expressed on a number of occasions, as the hon. member may know, and as certainly his wife will know, my concern about the lack of recreation space afforded to a project which has 120 units and houses well over 500 children.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
In addition to the compliments paid by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) to the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Clancy) I think he forgot to say he also had good voting habits.
I think the quality of this debate has been excellent. This is a very important subject and it has been dealt with, I think, in a constructive and useful way by all members who have taken part. I should like to say this because in recent weeks it has been the habit to be extremely critical of this parliament. Yet here we have legislation dealing with real problems, and there is no doubt the house can rise to the occasion and deal with these problems in an effective way.
I wish to go on record as agreeing with the remarks made by my hon. friend from Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I also come from a northern constituency, not quite as far north
National Housing Act
as he does but far enough north that to a limited extent the problems which his people face are those faced by the people of my area, too. I do hope that the minister, who I saw paying close attention when the hon. member for Yukon was speaking, will pay regard to his reasonable suggestions.
I should like to make one further observation, though it is not completely pertinent to this legislation before us. The $500 bonus program is one which does not apply in the north in the fullest way, northern winters being what they are. When the cut-off date comes we too often find that the weather has been so inclement that it has been impossible to reach the stage which could be expected in areas of Canada further to the south. This is very important. I have received a number of letters from people in my area who are anxious to take advantage of this provision, but unfortunately they have not been able to do so. While I agree there cannot be flexibility in legislation of this kind sufficient to satisfy the requirements of all the areas of Canada, I think the situation which arises in the northern regions should be given special consideration.
I listened with interest, too, to what was said by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott). I agree with much of what he said but I do not go along with him when he suggests that this matter might be the subject of a royal commission. This problem of housing and urban redevelopment is one which is extremely rapid in its occurrence and its changes and I do think that if you set up a royal commission, by the time this commission were to draw its conclusions the assumptions upon which those conclusions were based would no longer be valid. I am sure those members who have played any part in municipal government will bear with me when I say that frequently, from the time a municipal project is conceived, financed and carried through the necessary levels of government to the day of its conclusion, a considerable time has elapsed, and the end which the project was initially planned to serve has also extended.
So it would be with a royal commission. I would make this suggestion, however, and it is one I have made before. The standing committees of this house-and this, of course, is a subject for a committee which Your Honour and I are concerned with also-no longer are related to the exigencies of present day needs, and I should like to see a standing or select committee dedicated to the problem of urban redevelopment and housing This is a need which could be met by simple means at this time and, in conjunction, rather than a royal commission I should like to see a per-

National Housing Act
manent committee composed of the representatives of the three levels of government, federal, municipal and provincial. This would be a committee sitting continuously with a permanent secretariat to study these problems which arise from day to day, from week to week and from month to month. Liaison between that committee and the three levels of government would, I think, enable the machinery of government to be directed to at least a partial solution of the problems which have to do with housing and urban redevelopment.
Several years ago a measure of this kind was before this house. I had the honour to speak on that occasion and I want to repeat what I said then. I am going back, very briefly, to the amendments made to the National Housing Act in 1960, and I do this because the very problem I referred to then still exists; it has not been disposed of. We are still dealing with what, I submit, are the results and the effects of the problem and not with the real cause. At that time I was quoting from an article which appeared in Time magazine of August 29, 1960 and I should like, with permission, to quote part of this article again. The article was called "The Costly Earth" and it went on to say this:
The man who faces inflation's cruellest bite is the United States home builder-
And this can certainly be applied in this country.
-who starts off in search of land for his dream house.
Since 1950 the price of U.S. land for home building has soared anywhere from 100 per cent to 3,760 per cent-while building material prices have climbed a less spectacular 24 per cent and building trade wages 60 per cent.
I would imagine that this same comparison might well be made today. I did not secure statistics, because I did not know I would be speaking; but I think the same general trend would still apply. The article goes on:
In city and suburb alike, says House and Home the present tax structure harnesses the profit motive backward; it abets speculation, penalizes development. Underdeveloped land and vacant city lots are taxed, on the average, at less than 25 per cent valuation across the U.S. v. 40.8 per cent for business properties. Land, comprising one third of the U.S. national wealth, carries less than 5 per cent of the total tax load. Not surprisingly, land speculation has made more millionaires since world war II than any other form of U.S. business or investment.
If the U.S. is to avoid an even bigger land bust than in the '20s, concludes House and Home-
And this could certainly be applied in our country.
-cities and towns must act fast. Most experts agree that the first point of attack should be to ease the too-heavy tax burden on houses and other improvements, multiply the too-easy tax load on unimproved land, and make the unearned increment in land prices provide much

more of the taxes needed to provide the streets, water, sewer and schools without which unimproved land would be neither liveable nor saleable.
I had the honour of being present yesterday at the opening of an important conference having to do with the family, and I also heard the eloquent and articulate words which were spoken at that time to open the conference. Surely at the very root of this problem is the provision of adequate housing for the family. How can you have a family which fits into our civilization as we would like it to fit without having that family housed in suitable and reasonable circumstances? I do not know to what extent this conference is going to direct its attention to this problem, but I would hope that we in this house have an opportunity to do something about it, and we might well march with our proposals parallel to what is being done at the conference.
I am not being critical of the bill itself, because I support the principle and I think it will do a great deal to help solve the consequences which have flowed from the problem I mentioned; but I do not think it gets to the root cause. What runs in my mind, Mr. Speaker, is what the minister has said-and I agree very much with what he did say- along the same lines as the words spoken by the minister several years ago, when a companion piece of legislation to this was before this house and was passed. It is in my thinking that in the not too distant future we will be called back here to vote even larger sums of money to deal in an even more impressive way with this very grave problem of urban redevelopment, urban sprawl, the slums which continue to grow despite what is being done to dispose of them, the construction of schools, streets and sewers to facilitate servicing the houses which are required for our people. I am quite satisfied as I stand here and speak tonight that within a few years legislation of the same kind will be before us again. I recognize that the question of land taxation, of municipal taxation is one which lies, under our constitutional division of powers, exclusively within the jurisdiction of provincial governments, as does, of course, this business of housing and slum development. But by one of these flexible arrangements which our constitution permits between the three levels of government, we are tackling the one problem, and I hope in the course of the discussions the minister and his officials will be having from time to time with provincial governments they will have a look at the suggestion I am going to lay before him at this time. There have been for many years those who have advocated a different type of municipal tax. One school of thought with which I have some sympathy advocates the

approach of Henry George which, as it is related to municipal government, can be described as a method of tax by which the emphasis is shifted and the incidence is shifted from improvements to the land alone.
I am simply going to leave this thought with the minister and refer him to two studies which have been done in the last few years in connection with specific municipalities. One was done in the United Kingdom and was completed quite recently. It was published by the united committee for the taxation of land values. The survey was made on a voluntary basis by the rating and value association, and it was done in connection with the city of Whitstable in the United Kingdom. Then there is a research monograph completed in 1959 by Miss Mary Raw-son, who I think comes from the same city as does the minister. This is entitled "Property taxation and urban development". It covers a detailed analysis of urban development and taxation in the municipality of Burnaby, which of course is an area with which the minister is quite familiar. I am just going to read very briefly from this latter document; time will not permit me to do any more. But I would like the minister to give some attention to the summaries and conclusions contained therein.
This study was done very carefully. It was not a theoretical and philosophical discussion of the subject but, as is said in the foreword, it is-
-an able and well documented case study of what would happen in terms of land use and development in a municipality if the local ad valorem tax were shifted from land and improvements toward a land value tax.
The author comes well qualified, as the minister will know, for this sort of study. She is a native of British Columbia, a graduate of the University of British Columbia in economics and Slavonic studies, and was attached to the national research council of Canada for a period of years. In addition, she completed her master's thesis at the department of city and regional planning of the University of North Carolina. Let me conclude, Mr. Speaker, by just reading very briefly some of the conclusions, which I adopt as my wording and which I think are worthy of consideration. I shall read from page 27 of the monograph, which I will be glad to furnish to the minister if he is interested. First, dealing with the question of urban sprawl and the importance of increased land taxes, this study points out:
The importance of increased land taxes can probably best be appreciated in relation to the problem of sprawl-its extent and its cost to the community.
Sprawl is not a new phenomenon. Emil O. Jorgensen, writing in 1925, calculated that half the
National Housing Act
potential farming area and over half of our urban centres then consisted of vacant land.
There have been changes here, but I think that as related to value precisely the same proposition could be made:
It cost enough to build and maintain public improvements past all this unused land to reach people who were living further on, he said, but the amount of capital squandered, labour wasted and time consumed in passing and repassing these innumerable gaps of vacant land-daily, monthly, yearly-was "something appalling'' and, for the nation as a whole, "beyond all calculation or conjeetion".
This passage continues:
In 1938 Edmund Bacon described similar costs to the community in a study of Flint, Michigan. He counted 28,526 vacant lots (of which 43 per cent were tax delinquent) which were serviced with water and sewer at a cost of some $1,700,000.
Then later on:
The sprawl problem is almost purely the result of land speculation at work. Thousands of vacant service lots lie within our cities while thousands of new urban lots are offered in patches scattered about in the suburban and rural rings. The services which are sometimes said to be rendered by speculators in land pale into insignificance when judged against the resulting pattern of costs to the community.
I just put it in this way, that this can be seen by anyone who has been involved in the construction of houses in the last 10, 15 or 20 years and who has watched with interest the increase in the percentage of the cost of land as contrasted with the cost of the building itself which has gone into new homes. I can recall that when I first built a house I think probably 5 or 6 per cent of the cost was land. In the case of the last house I built it was nearer 25 per cent to 26 per cent; and there is no stopping this trend. Then dealing with slum clearance the study says:
In the slum, the process of natural renewal by private action has come to a stop, hindered, among other things, by speculation in land, and by the taxation of improvements.
It is my simple submission, Mr. Speaker, that the application of at least this principle in part would do more than anything else that I know of to compel the owners of what are now described as slum areas to bring into production those parcels of land in order to pay the taxes which would be necessarily involved in a scheme of this kind. Then we see:
To exempt improvements and at the same time to tax land more heavily would provide a double incentive to the owners of derelict buildings to demolish them and to use the land more intensively. Here surely is a golden key to urban renewal, to the automatic regeneration of the city- and not at public expense.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we have in this country an active and efficient housing industry. I think that more than any other

National Housing Act
industry in this country we are geared to do the sort of things which should be done, yet we find it necessary to come back time after time to the government for the kind of help which this legislation is going to give. This report continues:
To relieve dwellings of taxation removes a brake on investment which might take the form either of repair or of new construction. How great an improvement in the housing situation would result over time from this changed pressure, it is not possible to calculate.
This is, of course, a long range program. It may be four, five or six years before he or some other minister-and I expect it will be another minister-is going to ask the house for the passage of similar legislation. Therefore I would urge upon the minister and his officials the need to take a look at the problem. While I acknowledge the fact that it is completely out of his control to put into effect this type of tax situation, certainly at a conference he could bring it to the attention of municipal and provincial governments. He could also bring it to the attention of his colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) who, when urged for further funds by provincial governments, might well be able to point out the tremendously large amount of tax dollars going down the sewer from taxation of land speculation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intention is to speak very briefly to the bill we have before us and to bring up several points which I think are gross injustices with regard to the outworking of this legislation which is provided under the National Housing Act, the amendments to which are contained in Bill No. C-102. Shelter is of equal importance to the well-being of an individual in a free society, as is food itself. In fact, I am convinced that one of the best assurances for the continuance of a free way of life in a democratic society is the provision made within that society for direct home ownership. Much has been done in Canada in this regard, but we are yet far short of the desirable ideal so far as making it possible for individual citizens to own their own homes.
While it is not directly related to the amendments before us at the present time, I think we all agree that our tax system is antiquated so far as the home owner is concerned. Too often is he penalized for improving his own home and property, instead of being given the incentive to do this very thing. Second, the cost of financing home ownership is far too high. We speak about social capital and the need to provide capital without the heavy load of interest which we must pay today for the development of certain of our social capital needs. I am con-
IMr. Baldwin.]
vinced that home ownership fits into this category as well. I believe that one of the reforms which must be brought about in the future is the classification of capital, so far as that which is required to provide for the construction of homes for our citizens is concerned, on the same basis that we are coming to regard social capital used for general social development needs.
As an illustration of this present problem a $12,000 mortgage on a home costs a homeowner after 20 years $21,326, on the basis that he is paying 6J per cent interest on the money. After 25 years it costs him $24,114. It means that in just 25 years the cost of financing his home is more than the cost of the construction of his home. At the end of 30 years this amount has been raised to $27,060. This does not include many of the other charges which are part of financing a home under the provisions of the National Housing Act, which is the authority which sets up Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
It is not my intention to go into detail on this subject because I want to bring into focus several injustices which are included in the present operation of the act about which I do not think very many of us have thought too much. Therefore, I will briefly deal with certain procedures established by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and followed by mortgage companies in Canada which appear to me to be contrary to the law and which work a considerable injustice upon many of our Canadian citizens whose homes are subject to these mortgages.
One of the requirements of a mortgage authorized by the corporation is that the monthly instalments shall be increased by an arbitrary amount, to cover the cost of insurance on the mortgaged property; likewise that amount which is intended to cover the municipal taxes to be paid on the property. This amount is always estimated and is always in excess of the actual amount of the taxes levied and the cost of insurance involved.
A more serious objection, however, is that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is endeavouring to interfere in a way which I think transgresses provincial laws in attempting to set itself up as a compulsory agent between the mortgagor and mortgagee with respect to taxes imposed by a municipal authority. It is not possible for C.M.H.C. to make the mortgagor the agent of the taxing authority, so therefore it must endeavour to make the mortgagee the agent of the mortgagor. It is a rule of law that agencies may be terminated by the principal at will subject to the payment of any damages for breach of agency contract if such damages in fact exist;

but no contract of an agency can be made irrevocable. In this case the mortgagee is attempting to claim the right to intervene between a taxing authority and a taxpayer against the wishes of the taxpayer and to occupy a position distinct from that of the agent of the taxpayer. This position is unknown in the normal procedures of civil law. For many centuries it has not been constitutionally possible to farm out the collection of taxes to anybody.
A further serious objection to the system is that the agent of the mortgagor can only be a trustee holding moneys on behalf of the taxpayer until the time they are paid to the taxing authority. During this period any interest earned by the money actually belongs to the taxpayers and should be credited to his mortgage account. The appropriation by the mortgagee of such interest constitutes legalized embezzlement. It is not difficult to see that the present system provides the mortgagee with large sums of the taxpayer's money for its own use to the date of payment of the taxes, and it has apparently been the practice for many years for all lending institutions to appropriate, or perhaps it is better to say misappropriate, the interest on such moneys.
There can be no objection to the mortgagor adopting such an arrangement when he so desires, but to have it forced upon him is another question altogether. There should be no way of depriving him of the right to refuse such an arrangement or to terminate it in order to pay his taxes himself directly to the taxing authority whenever he sees fit to do so. But this is not his prerogative under the present arrangement. From my own experience in this regard the lending institutions will exert every pressure possible, by intimidation or otherwise, to discourage the mortgagor from exercising these very fundamental rights.
A further abuse to be found in the regulations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and which is related to the particular amendments before us at the present time, has to do with the fact that the mortgagor is obliged to carry fire insurance to the full face value of his mortgage. The mortgage, however, is secured by both the building and the land, and I do not think any insurance company will ever issue insurance coverage on land itself. Usually this represents an increasing proportion of the mortgage starting at approximately one third. It can be readily seen that by this means the premiums are greatly and artificially inflated over and above the cost of financing the mortgage itself, as I referred to in my earlier remarks. Since insurance companies flatly
National Housing Act
refuse to value a structure by itself for insurance purposes and will accept coverage only on the full face value of the mortgage. The mortgagor is thus effectively prevented from determining how much fire insurance should equitably be carried on the building subject to the mortgage.
These may seem to be minor points, Mr. Speaker, but in my opinion they amount to the robbing of those who finance their homes under the provisions of this act of many millions of dollars a year simply because of the fact that under these regulations the financing institution is able to carry on these unfair and inequitable practices. The public are left wholly without protection in this situation since few can afford the cost of litigation and in most cases the cost of litigation would far exceed the amount taken from the home owner through the application of these procedures.
I think something ought to be done to correct this situation. I urge the government to look into the matter because while the point may appear a minor one in many respects, it is a fundamental right of the home owner that is being transgressed. What we ought to be doing in this legislation and through the whole policy involved under the national housing administration is to encourage rather than discourage the private ownership of homes.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two observations in taking part in this very useful debate that has been going on this evening. The subject of homes in which people live affects the lives of a great many in this country. I well recall my first session in the house in 1957 when the Conservative government introduced legislation to increase the funds available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in order to make it possible to build more homes and to create more jobs. We all recall what wonderful effects this action had on the creation of jobs throughout Canada. I should like to commend the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) for his suggestion with regard to setting up a standing committee of the house on housing. I think this is an excellent idea and I hope the house will give consideration to the suggestion.
There are only two or three sections about which I should like to ask the minister questions at this stage of the bill. The first has to do with urban redevelopment. I apologize for not having been able to follow the minister too closely, and I hope he will correct me if I am wrong in what I say. I understand that first of all a city has to designate the area. First, who designates the area?

National Housing Act Is it the city itself, the province or the corporation? When an area is designated, does it have to be a slum area in order for a person to be able to get a loan on an existing house? In my own city there is an area three or four blocks wide where some of the oldest and finest homes of the city are situated. These are homes that people would like to buy if they could get a loan with which to purchase them. At the present time it is very difficult to get loans on such houses. However, if this area is designated I understand that C.M.H.C. will grant loans on the existing houses so that people can buy these fine old homes and convert them into duplexes or live in them as they are, or perhaps fix them up to their former condition and appearance.
If it is not made possible for people to get loans on older houses, then in view of the development of the urban sprawl in all cities across Canada I am sure almost anyone can visualize that some of the fine old sections of the cities of Canada will become slum areas. I hope the new provision is not set up in such a way that the area has to be designated a slum area before people can get loans to buy these houses.
In June, 1960, the former minister of public works, Hon. David Walker, made it possible for universities to get loans at the rate of 51 per cent in order to build dormitories on university campuses. This provision has been used to a great extent. I am sorry I do not have the figures for 1964 but as of June, 1963, some $49 million had been advanced for this purpose. I am sure the amount must be nearly double by now. I commend the minister for improving this section so that student cooperatives will now be able to obtain loans under the act. With the great development of universities throughout Canada and the tremendous difficulties that universities are having in providing accommodation for their students, I am sure that student co-operatives will use this provision to a great extent.
There are many student co-operatives on campuses throughout Canada. In my own community of Guelph there is a student cooperative at the university which is most anxious to see the bill passed so that it can make application for a loan to build a student dormitory. In many of these co-operative residences students are able to work a few hours each week toward the cost of their accommodation. I am sure this provision in the act will fill a long needed want.
Another point I should like to make has to do with loans to non-profit organizations to build residences for senior citizens. This provision has been in the act for some time and in my view there has been a little window dressing in making reference to it in the


resolution. However, I should like to see this section of the act used to a greater extent because it is really appalling to see the rooms in which some of our senior citizens have to live. There is a great opportunity here to provide better accommodation for our senior citizens.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the minister's attention to the inspection aspect of C.M.H.C. operations. I know they sell what are called approved homes, but quite often purchasers of N.H.A. homes have brought to my attention flaws and poor construction in their homes. Only this week end a constituent told me that he had bought an N.H.A. home. I believe he is the second or third owner. It is a split level design and in the construction the builders failed to use enough gravel in the back part that is built on the ground. The result is that the whole floor has caved in and the plumbing, baseboards and flooring have caved in or deteriorated. This house is only eight years old. So this inspection of buildings is most important. I am sure the corporation will give every attention to this very necessary part of the construction of homes for the safeguarding of our Canadian people. I commend the minister on opening the National Housing Act for amendments, and this party is most happy to see these amendments put into effect.

entirely qualified to establish a certain distinction between the climate in the western provinces and in the eastern part of this country.
Mr. Speaker, we will soon celebrate the centenary of confederation, and I wonder whether the government could not exempt from interest the towns and municipalities which would want to take advantage of the services offered by C.M.H.C. to demolish slums within their limits and replace them by new, cleaner and healthier housing.
We know that slums are a liability for this country because, first of all, investigations have revealed that they mostly are a breeding ground for juvenile delinquency, for it is there that we find the highest delinquency and crime rate. Second, municipal assessment is very low in slum areas and, consequently, municipalities stand to lose a lot; third, insurance rates are higher in slum areas which are considered a bad risk. Fourth, there are more frequent and more numerous fires in such areas. Consequently, slums constitute a liability for cities and towns and, therefore, for the whole country.

He said certain builders were bypassing or getting round the regulations of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and he wanted to know what steps were being taken to prevent this practice. I am sure the hon. member is familiar with regulation 20 of the national housing regulations which provides that an approved loan shall be made by an approved lender to a borrower at no less than the par value thereof, and that the borrower shall not be subjected to a charge in the nature of a discount or commission.
I am informed by C.M.H.C. that there has been the odd case within the last few months -that is to say, one or two cases-where it has been alleged that a builder-borrower has been subjected to a commission. These cases are being investigated. I might say that this act, as hon. members know, has been working for many years and we have had no difficulty whatever with the approved lenders who have

been functioning for any appreciable length of time. There have been difficulties with new lenders who have been approved recently and our present information is that the incidents referred to by the hon. member are cases involving new approved lenders. I can assure him that we will take action in this regard.
I would like at the outset, Mr. Speaker, to thank all hon. members for their kind words of appreciation of the co-operation they have received from the officials of C.M.H.C. It bears out the opinion I have formed of them in the two and a half months I have been the minister reporting for the corporation to the house. I also want to thank hon. members for their kind references to myself, and I can only express the hope that I may be able to live up to the expectations some of my hon. friends have put forward on my behalf. I will do my best.
I must say that I was very impressed with the remarks of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott). He made a number of constructive suggestions. I think the most important comment he made was, "The question is not what is going to happen here as to the passing of this bill, but what is going to happen after the bill becomes law". I agree with him. The proof of the pudding will be in the eating, what counts is what is done after the amendments are accepted by this house, as I hope they will be at a very early date. The hon. member suggested that a royal commission might be set up to have a look at urban Canada, as he described it, and study the problems of the low income families and our senior citizens or elderly people. I would rather give that suggestion some thought.
Another hon. member of the official opposition suggested that we have a permanent committee of this house do the same thing. I can assure the house through you, Mr. Speaker, that these suggestions will receive careful consideration.
The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) and one hon. member, who preceded him, complained about red tape. I practised law long enough before I went into business to know something of the difficulties caused by red tape, and I can assure the hon. member that I will do my part to see to it that if there is any red tape that is interfering with the sound administration of this act, I will do my best to see that the red tape is cut. With regard to the suggestion that a separate department of urban growth and development be set up, my only comment is that I know both hon. members who suggested this appreciate the difficulties that lie in the way. They said they appreciated there were difficulties. Having regard to the difficulties that you run into when you try
National Housing Act
to get the provinces to accept amendments such as are incorporated in this bill-and the course agreed upon represents months of careful negotiation. Hon. members will recall some of the difficulties we ran into with the municipal loan development fund. With property and civil rights in the background-the field in which a minister responsible for urban growth and development could work would be rather restricted, I would think. However, the matter will be considered, but I do not want to offer hon. members too much encouragement at this time. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce raised a question with regard to section 36(b). That is something that I think could be more effectively dealt with in the clause by clause discussion.
I would appreciate it if the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) would send me the second of the two studies to which he referred, namely the research monograph. It sounded like interesting reading. The hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) asked, "Are loans under the proposed legislation limited to existing houses in designated areas?" The strict answer is yes, but loans are not limited to slums or near slum areas. A designated area, as I explained in my opening remarks, and as will be seen from the provisions of the act, could be a blighted area or an area in which there has been an indication that blight may or is likely to set in. Under those circumstances either the province or the municipality designated by the province could designate a blighted area-not necessarily a slum area. I think this is what was troubling the hon. member.
I see that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) has left the chamber, but he referred to the fact that he wanted to put housing in the west on the same footing as it is in the east. He overlooks the fact that we have some cold weather in the west, too. I can refer him to the interior parts of British Columbia and to the Yukon, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. He will find that we have problems there which are even greater than they have in parts of eastern Canada.
With regard to one of the two points raised by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton), I would say this. He referred to the fact that the government promised to extend loans to existing houses. I think, in fairness, the hon. member will agree that while we have not extended them to existing houses in all parts of the country, we have made an encouraging start at least by including existing houses in areas that are designated as needing attention. Any other

National Housing Act

APPOINTMENT TO COMMISSION OF WIFE OF CABINET MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 22 last I asked the Prime Minister the following question:
Does he approve of the appointment to the conference on the centennial of confederation of the wife of the Minister of Forestry, who is already an employee of the C.B.C. and who did not even take the trouble of attending the meeting held in Charlottetown last April 25 and 26?
Mr. Speaker, the wife of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) is the moderator of many programs of opinion for the C.B.C. I cannot do otherwise than denounce this family compact. The Minister of Forestry has emoluments of $35,000 a year and his wife receives from the C.B.C. approximately $15,000 a year. Moreover, she is a member of the national centennial commission.
Mr. Speaker, in the opinion of the great majority of C.B.C. listeners, it is a scandal. And yet, Mr. Lesage, who was elected to office in Quebec, ordered royal investigations on peccadillos.


Mr. Speaker, the majority of listeners of the French C.B.C. network feel that we are faced with a real scandal, since it is the same family which controls and receives from a crown corporation and the government a very large amount of money.
Mr. Speaker, the wife of the Minister of Forestry embarrasses the employees of the C.B.C. and her presence in that corporation represents another type of blackmail for the authorities of the C.B.C., who do not dare dismiss her. In fact, what would happen if the head of the service concerned would dare dismiss the wife of a minister of the crown? The C.B.C. is wrongly considered as a den or the Mecca of the Liberal party on account of the wife of the Minister of Forestry.
When the Minister of Forestry discusses with his colleagues during a meeting of the cabinet the budget of the C.B.C., how do you want him to be unbiased and to protect the interests of the C.B.C. when his wife collects fabulous fees from that corporation.
Mr. Speaker, Caesar's wife must be beyond reproach. Caesar Sauve, save Caesar. Caesar's wife should not be open to suspicion, even if these suspicions amount to $15,000 to $20,000 per year collected from the C.B.C. while her husband, Caesar Sauve, gets $35,000 a year as minister of the crown.
Mr. Speaker, over the week end His Excellency the Governor General opened a conference on the Canadian family. We are all in favour of clannishness, but after all, is the family compact of Caesar Sauve not making a great deal of money at the expense of the 600,000 unemployed of Canada? Mrs. Jeanne Sauve, wife of the Minister of Forestry, will perhaps become the Cleopatra of the twentieth century.
Mr. Speaker, it is time the government took a position. Most Canadian taxpayers object to the wife of the Minister of Forestry collecting fabulous fees from the C.B.C. while her husband is a minister of the crown and a member of the cabinet.
How do you expect the situation not to be embarrassing for the C.B.C. officials who dare not dismiss her for fear that their own heads might roll as a result of their action, since they are faced with a powerful man, a powerful government which intervenes often directly and indirectly in the affairs of C.B.C., as we found out lately.
Mr. Speaker, the 600,000 Canadian unemployed are justified in complaining about that situation, and I hope that the Canadian government is going to face up to its responsibilities and break off that family compact which is so shameful for our country.

AUTHORITY FOR FLOODING BEHIND DAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is not of quite such a personal nature as the previous one, but it is one which concerns national interests. The other day I asked the minister the following question:
Has the B.C. hydro and power authority asked the minister for his approval for the flooding of the reservoir behind the Peace river dam without

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the removal of forest growth and vegetation except for the partial clearing of certain channels necessary to meet the requirements for very limited navigation?
I asked that question because of the concern of a number of people in British Columbia in the conservation of our natural resources, and because we are quite reliably informed that the B.C. hydro authority, because of certain expenses and circumstances that exist, intends to destroy several billion feet of timber without removing it from the basin. With this will go a certain destruction of fish and wildlife, with certain impediments to navigation, and also with a great destruction of the aesthetic values, or what I should call the intangible values, which we have discussed in recent weeks in the external affairs committee.
This matter was brought to my attention by a friend of mine who was very close to the B.C. hydro authority, and I notice several questions have been asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets), with respect to the same question as to whether a licence had been issued for the building of this dam.
As recorded at page 2832 of Hansard for May 1, the Minister of Public Works said this:
Hon. members will recall that months ago we had secured an opinion from the Department of Justice to make sure that at the point of dam construction the Peace river was navigable. The question has also been raised as to whether the legislation as it stands is binding on the crown in the right of a province. These are questions of legal interpretation as to the precise terms of the Navigable Waters Protections Act. There are a number of amendments to that act that would be desirable, and when they are brought forward action will be recommended to remove the uncertainty to which I have referred, and to make clear the extent of the application of the act. In the immediate case, as the project is now under construction, a licence cannot be applied for, under the terms of the act, until the work is completed.
Then he went on to say, as recorded on the next page:
It is intended to review this information with the British Columbia hydro and power authority to make sure there is no risk of prejudice to navigation and, as I said previously, amendments to the act would be desirable to remove the uncertainties; and we intend to introduce such amendments. In the meantime there exists complete co-operation with the British Columbia hydro and power authority to ensure security of navigation in the area. I hope this information will be found satisfactory by those hon. members most interested in the matter.
As a matter of fact, the matter is still in uncertain circumstances. When I received this information from Victoria I got in touch with the Department of Public Works and they informed me they had received certain

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion communications from the B.C. hydro authority. I told them I intended to ask this question, but just before coming into the house at 2.30 I was advised I should ask this question of the Department of Transport, as it was now handling the matter. I did ask the Acting Minister of Transport and my question was ruled out of order. That is why I am speaking now. Tonight I see the genial minister of northern affairs (Mr. Laing) is prepared to leap to his feet to answer my question, but this all indicates, shall I say, a sense of ambiguity as to who is responsible for this information. I am sure that when we have heard from the minister we will have more information than we have had to date.
I want him to answer the following questions. (1) Has the British Columbia hydro power authority applied for a licence to build a dam, and when? (2) What are the specifications of the procedure to be followed in clearing the basin of its timber resources, and are they intending to issue a licence and permit B.C. hydro authority to destroy billions of feet of merchantable timber; did they apply for a licence to flood this timber and at the same time to cut various channels needed to permit navigation on certain areas in this long basin which, I understand, is close to 250 miles in extent? (3) Can the minister report any progress with respect to the application of B.C. hydro for this permit?
We are concerned about this. We should like to get answers and we intend to follow it up closely. We are of the opinion that what happens on the Peace river will establish a pattern to be followed on the Columbia, and we want to make certain that these resources are properly dealt with. We want to protect our wildlife by making certain that the natural resources of the Peace river are protected and that an application for a licence is not complied with until this government has an assurance that the basin will be cleared according to standards proposed by the fish and game federation of British Columbia, and the rod and gun clubs of the interior of British Columbia, the west Kootenay and the east Kootenay. I look forward to the minister's reply and perhaps we will go away better informed than we are to date.
